13689.text: "They were enraged" (Act 7:54) is diapriō ("to be sawn through", G1282) with kardia ("heart"); "they ground their teeth at him" puts the anger in the body; against them stands Stephen, "full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven" (7:55); the M47 token is the heart word itself.

13692.text: Num 20:13 names Meribah: "where the people of Israel quarreled with the Lord, and through them he showed himself holy".

13698.text: The teeth are where anger and hostility show, as the hands are for fear: "The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away" (Psa 112:10); "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psa 37:12); and Act 7:54.

13703.text: Links that do not count are non-inner-being senses of the M47 word: Pro 25:23, Eze 13:13, 19:12 and Psa 11:6 (wind); Num 11:33 (meat); Eze 16:26 (lustful "flesh"); Eze 7:19 (nephesh as hunger); Psa 124:5 ("us"); Est 8:11 (lives as targets); no M02 Strong's loses its implicit status through this.

13707.text: Divine wrath in Revelation (14:10, 19; 15:1, 7; 16:1, 19; 19:15) becomes a substance: wine, a cup, bowls, a winepress; the human side is drinking it (14:10; 16:19); in Rev 14:8 and 18:3 "the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality" the same word means intoxicating passion, and the drinking image is shared with God's wrath.

13712.text: 2Cor 7:11 lists "what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal" as the fruit of "godly grief", a sequence of inner operations valued as good; Mar 10:14 is Jesus's indignation, and the bearer class is recorded as divine in the party data, noted and not resolved.

13726.text: The strife words are mostly in vice lists and church-order texts, where the inner place is given by the frame: 1Cor 3:3, "you are still of the flesh"; 1Ti 6:4-5, "puffed up with conceit ... depraved in mind" (nous is excluded from M47 by ruling 4, so these do not count as seated); Gal 5:26 ("provoking one another, envying one another") sits between 5:24-25 (flesh crucified, walk by the Spirit) and 6:1.

13730.text: Meribah is a place name that stores an inner event ("the waters of Meribah, where the people of Israel quarreled with the Lord", Num 20:13); in Eze 47:19 and 48:28 it is a boundary marker with no inner content left; in Psa 106:32 the next verse is seated (106:33, "they made his spirit bitter", Moses's spirit).

13744.text: The wisdom sayings treat anger as governable from outside: "a soft answer turns away wrath" (Pro 15:1); "a gift in secret averts anger" (21:14); "the wise turn away wrath" (29:8); "a wise man will appease" the king's wrath (16:14); Jam 1:19-20, "slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God", followed at once by "the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (1:21, seated).

13756.text: God's own seat in resolve and purpose, none of it hardened: he "said in his heart, 'I will never again curse the ground'" (Gen 8:21); "what is in my heart" (1Sa 2:35); "a man after his own heart" (1Sa 13:14; Act 13:22); "my eyes and my heart will be there" (1Ki 9:3; 2Ch 7:16); 2Ki 10:30; 1Ch 17:19; Psa 33:11; "the day of vengeance was in my heart" (Isa 63:4); "the intents of his heart" (Jer 23:20; 30:24); "with all my heart and all my soul" (Jer 32:41); Job 7:17; 10:13; 34:14.

13758.text: God's own seat in delight and aversion, none of it hardened: "my soul delights" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18); "his soul hates the wicked" (Psa 11:5); "an abomination to his soul" (Pro 6:16); "my soul hates ... I am weary of bearing them" (Isa 1:14); "I abhor the pride of Jacob" (Amo 6:8, sworn "by himself"); "my soul has no pleasure in him" (Heb 10:38); "my soul will abhor you" (Lev 26:30; negated in 26:11); "the beloved of my soul" handed over (Jer 12:7); the human question "Does your soul loathe Zion?" (Jer 14:19).

13760.text: Jer 15:1 is probably the text behind the recollection of God's heart hardening: it is the only verse found where God's own seat is turned away; beside it stand the aversion texts Lev 26:30; Psa 11:5; Isa 1:14; Amo 6:8.

13764.text: The same root, used of God, means glory: kaved, "to be heavy", is the word for Pharaoh's hardened heart (Exo 8:15, 32; 9:34; 10:1), and in the same narrative God says "I will harden [chazaq] Pharaoh's heart ... and I will get glory [kaved] over Pharaoh" (Exo 14:4, 17); the root that makes the human heart heavy makes God glorious (also Lev 10:3; Isa 26:15; Hag 1:8; Eze 28:22; 39:13).

13774.text: Mat 25:24-26: "Master, I knew you to be a hard man"; the servant names the source of his perception himself, "so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent" (25:25); the master answers "You wicked and slothful servant!" (25:26): the perception of hardness is born of fear, and the parable condemns it.

13779.text: The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Righteousness and justice, with steadfast love and faithfulness: "You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand … Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you" (Psa 89:13–14). "The Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (Dan 9:14), then "who brought your people out … with a mighty hand" (9:15), then "according to all your righteous acts, let your anger … turn away" (9:16)

13789.text: The heaviness has its source in God's character: the texts name righteousness and justice (Psa 89:14; Dan 9:14, 16) together with steadfast love, faithfulness, the oath, and the cause of the weak; anger is named too, but never as the last word, standing inside a purpose of covenant, atonement and healing.

13793.text: Meribah as a place name: the verses about the people's quarrel are human (Exo 17:7; Num 20:13, 24; 27:14; Deu 32:51); in Deu 33:8 and Psa 81:7 God does the striving or testing, and these are divine; the pure boundary markers (Eze 47:19; 48:28) have no inner being.

13803.text: 2Cor 7:11 (5V Indignation produced by godly grief): indignation and fear as fruits of godly grief.

13824.text: Psa 55:3 (U Enemies' anger, as the one attacked bears it): the one attacked: "My heart is in anguish within me".

13832.text: Dan 11:30 (4S Anger against one suspected or set against): afraid, then enraged.

13868.text: 1Ti 2:8 (5M A person's anger governed: be angry and do not sin; slow to anger; at a brother; in prayer; in the overseer; not in love): prayer without anger or quarrelling.

13887.text: Zep 2:3, "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord": the call comes before "the burning anger of the Lord" (2:2); the people called are already humble and already doing his commands, and are told to seek humility; the verse promises nothing, "perhaps"; being hidden is God's act.

13892.text: Pro 11:4, "Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death": the day of wrath tests what a person has relied on; the next verses go on, "The righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight" (11:5), and "the treacherous are taken captive by their lust" (11:6).

13895.text: Anger comes where a lifted state is checked: the heart lifted by strength (Uzziah), the merry heart (Ahasuerus), the glad heart (Haman), the heart already set (Dan 11:28).

13897.text: Fear and anger follow one another: anger at God, then fear of God (2Sa 6:8–9); fear first, then anger at a weaker target (Dan 11:30).

13922.text: Outside the verse: no seat in Gen 45:2–9 or Job 18:1–7.

13927.text: Num 23:10 "Let me [my nephesh] die the death of the upright". Genuine. The would-be pronouncer's own.

13932.text: 2Ti 2:22 "a pure heart". Genuine. The remedy's site. The seat appears as the remedy (the pure heart, the Spirit) or as the victim (the naive heart). The quarreller's own source is named as passions, flesh or conceit, not as a seat word. This parallels M20 v3 §20 point 2: the seat as the site of the remedy.

13949.text: Outside: Psa 7:9–10 "hearts" / "upright in heart" (D v2 §1.1, §11; E v2 §8.1, §11.3). Isa 30:29 "gladness of heart".

13950.text: Seat (v3). Outside: Eze 36:5 "wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (heart and nephesh). Edom's. Genuine. Hab 3:16's "body" and "bones" carry no M47 tag in the DB, so they are bodily trembling and not a counted seat.

13953.text: Seat (v2). Outside: Psa 86:13 "you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol". The pleader's own. Genuine (E v2 §10.1, §11.3).

13970.text: Outside: Psa 78:37 "heart" (E v2 §5.1, §7.1); 78:39 "flesh … wind"; Isa 57:15 (C v3 §8.4; D v2 §10.2; G v3 §2 and others). Nothing new.

13972.text: Seat (v3). Outside: Eze 14:20 "their own lives" (nephesh). Life-sense. Eze 22:25 "devoured human lives".

14007.text: Psa 10:13 "say in his heart". The offender's.

14010.text: Where it comes from. Thirst, and doubt of God's presence (17:1–7). For Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not believe in me" (Num 20:12). The people's quarrel is answered in the leaders by unbelief, and the leaders' act at the rock (20:10–11: "Hear now, you rebels", striking twice) takes the quarrel into themselves.

14012.text: With a turned wish: the hired curser ends by wishing for the end of those he was hired to curse, "Let me die the death of the upright" (Num 23:10; G v3 §16.2; H v1 §6.5).

14026.text: With its named opposites: "that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment" (1Cor 1:10); "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6); "the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone … correcting his opponents with gentleness" (2Ti 2:24–25); "keep in step with the Spirit" (Gal 5:25).

14042.text: What it leads to. "At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter" (2Cor 7:11). The comfort of the other: "his spirit has been refreshed by you all" (7:13). Meeting together and encouraging (Heb 10:25).

14050.text: Whose spirit is not determinable. The M47 spirit classification v2 marks Psa 106:33 as [U] (#1880 item C-R4; C v3 R4). It could be Moses' spirit embittered, or God's Spirit rebelled against (compare Isa 63:10). Either way, the verse ties Meribah to Moses' loss "on their account".

14054.text: The king who trusts: "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5).

14057.text: What it leads to. The people are spared. In Deuteronomy, the memory of the intercession is itself turned into instruction (Deu 9:25–29, "So I lay prostrate …"), set against the people's claim to righteousness (§8).

14058.text: absent: "there was no one to intercede" (Isa 59:16; §41).

14101.text: Humbling with a confession of God's justice: "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); "you are just" (Ezr 9:15).

14104.text: 1Ki 8:47–48 / 2Ch 6:37–38 "turn their heart … with all their heart and with all their soul" (B v3 §5; C v3 §2.3, §8.1; D v2 §5; E v2 §13).

14130.text: "Our holy and beautiful house … has been burned by fire" (Isa 64:11).

14143.text: Pride: "I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless" (Isa 13:11).

14170.text: the heart that rejoices when protected (§3; Isa 30:29; 66:14).

14172.text: Daniel's confession resting on mercy, not righteousness (Dan 9:18).

14187.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: Anger lodges, and where it lodges is named. "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools" (Ecc 7:9). This joins Job 36:13 ("cherish anger"). Anger that stays has a lodging, and the lodging is the fool's. The verse before sets up the pair: "the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit" (7:8); Its duration is limited to a day: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil" (Eph 4:26–27). Where Gen 27 waited years for anger to turn away, the NT sets a limit of one day. The reason given is what anger left overnight opens: "opportunity to the devil"; It repeats: "A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again" (Pro 19:19). Great wrath is a pattern, not an event. Rescue does not end it; It is weighed:; "A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both" (Pro 27:3). This echoes Job's "heavier than the sand of the sea"; "Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?" (Pro 27:4). Anger is measured, and jealousy is found to be worse; Jealousy makes it unappeasable: "jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation" (Pro 6:34–35). This is the one anger in Proverbs that a gift will not avert. Compare §23: "A gift in secret averts anger" (Pro 21:14); It shows at once: "The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult" (Pro 12:16). The fool's anger cannot be hidden, while the prudent one lets the insult pass unanswered; It is where the wicked end up: "the expectation of the wicked [ends] in wrath".

14196.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The four strands hold, and each gains an instance: Strand (a), a demand no one can meet, with the angry one now the demander. "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand … no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Dan 2:10–11). Then "Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (2:12). This is the mirror of Gen 30:2. Jacob, faced with an impossible demand, named God as the only one who could meet it. Nebuchadnezzar hears the same answer ("except the gods") and orders a massacre; The anger is answered by "prudence and discretion" (Dan 2:14): Daniel's; Strand (b), thwarted and made a fool of. "Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children" (Mat 2:16). "Tricked" is Balaam's "you have made a fool of me" (Num 22:29). This time the killing is carried out, and it ends in "Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted" (Mat 2:18); Strand (d), refused by subordinates; Nebuchadnezzar "in furious rage" at the three who "do not serve your gods" (Dan 3:12–13); After their answer, "But if not … we will not serve your gods" (3:18), "Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more" (3:19); The face changes outward, against them. This is the reverse of §1's fallen face, which turns inward; The outcome reverses the anger: "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego … who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command" (3:28). The king blesses the very refusal that enraged him; A new instance, thwarted from outside and turned against the weaker: "ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant" (Dan 11:30). "News from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy" (11:44). Fear comes first, then anger. The anger is turned on a weaker target than the one that thwarted him.

14197.text: Seat . No in-verse seat in the six: Outside the verse: Dan 11:28 "his heart shall be set against the holy covenant". Genuine. The bearer's own, two verses before the rage. The heart was set before the thwarting. The anger only releases it; Dan 2:11 "not with flesh". Spurious as a seat: flesh as the human realm.

14217.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The one wronged is now God, or God's law, rather than a sister, a friend or the poor: The indignation seizes its bearer: "Hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law" (Psa 119:53). The bearer is its object as well as its subject. It is framed between comfort in God's rules (119:52) and "Your statutes have been my songs" (119:54). The indignation sits inside a life held by the law it defends; The spirit provoked by what it sees: "while Paul was waiting … his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue … and in the marketplace every day" (Act 17:16–17). This is the same movement as Neh 5:6–7: indignation, then an inner act, then public speech. Here the seat is named in the indignation verse itself; Annoyance that finally acts: the slave girl "kept doing this for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you … come out of her'" (Act 16:18); What annoys him is a true proclamation ("These men are servants of the Most High God", 16:17) from a wrong source; The anger builds over "many days" before the act; The act sets off anger in others: "when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas" (16:19).

14229.text: What it leads to. Joseph: reconciliation, and a summons to the father (45:9). Job: Bildad goes on to the fate of the wicked (18:5–7).

14230.text: Seat: In the verse: Job 18:4 "yourself" (nephesh). The bearer's own. Genuine, as the self that anger harms; Gen 45:5 "with yourselves" is literally "in your eyes" [lexical, not in DB]. It is not tagged as a seat in the DB. [verify] if the researcher wants the Hebrew checked; Outside the verse: no seat in Gen 45:2–9 or Job 18:1–7.

14237.text: What it does: It flares at the sight: "as soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses' anger burned hot" (Exo 32:19); It breaks what was given: "he threw the tablets … and broke them" (32:19); It destroys the object: the calf "burned … ground it to powder … made the people of Israel drink it" (32:20); It rebukes by question: "Why have you not eaten the sin offering …?" (Lev 10:17); "Have you let all the women live?" (Num 31:15); It states the limit that was missed: "You should have struck five or six times … now you will strike down Syria only three times" (2Ki 13:19).

14240.text: What it does: It tests God with a question: "they tested the Lord by saying, 'Is the Lord among us or not?'" (Exo 17:7); It nearly turns on the leader: "They are almost ready to stone me" (17:4); In the Numbers and Deuteronomy verses, Meribah is where the leaders themselves "rebelled against my command" (Num 20:24), "failing to uphold me as holy … before their eyes" (27:14), and "broke faith with me" (Deu 32:51).

14241.text: How it co-exists: With naming: the place becomes a memory. "He called the name of the place Massah and Meribah" (Exo 17:7), and "These are the waters of Meribah" (Num 20:13); With death sentences on the leaders, repeated at every mention: Aaron "shall not enter the land" (20:24), Moses "gathered to your people" (27:13), "die on the mountain" (Deu 32:50).

14254.text: How it co-exists: With a turned wish: the hired curser ends by wishing for the end of those he was hired to curse, "Let me die the death of the upright"; With Job's own hope, just before: "yet in my flesh I shall see God … My heart faints within me!" (Job 19:26–27).

14255.text: Seat: In the verse: none; Outside the verse:; Num 23:10 "Let me [my nephesh] die the death of the upright". Genuine. The would-be pronouncer's own; Job 19:27 "My heart [kidneys] faints within me". Genuine. The bearer's own, Job's, just before his warning. New here. Job 19:26 "in my flesh" is bodily, the flesh in which he will see God.

14276.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: The body's end of rivalrous anger: "The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!" (Psa 112:10). What he sees is the righteous man, whose "horn is exalted in honor" (112:9). Seeing the rival's rise ends in the angry one dissolving, not in the spear of 1Sa 18; Contrast seat: "His heart is steady; he will not be afraid" (112:8), said of the righteous one, two verses before. The seat is again named in the one the anger is aimed at (see Neh 4:6 above). Genuine; Rivalry among the disciples: "when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers" (Mat 20:24 = Mar 10:41). What they heard was Jesus's answer about the two brothers' place: "to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant" (Mat 20:23; Mar 10:40); Jesus answers by redefining greatness: "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them … It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant" (Mat 20:25–26; Mar 10:42–43); The anger at a rival's rise is not rebuked directly. The standing it is about is re-defined, so the rise it resented no longer counts. This is a reframing, the §9 and §6 move used on rivalry; Seat : none in-verse.

14278.text: What it does: It divides by allegiance: "there is quarreling among you … each one of you says, 'I follow Paul,' or 'I follow Apollos'" (1Cor 1:11–12); it creates obstacles: "those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine" (Rom 16:17); it breeds: "they breed quarrels" (2Ti 2:23); it spoils prayer: "lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1Ti 2:8).

14279.text: Where it comes from. Every verse, or the one next to it, names a source, and the sources are inner: Passions at war within: "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel" (Jam 4:1–2). The outer fight is the inner war carried outward; The flesh: "for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?" (1Cor 3:3), after "I could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh" (3:1); Conceit: "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26). "He is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy" (1Ti 6:4); Appetite: the dividers "do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites [belly]" (Rom 16:18); Envy and selfish ambition behind a good act: "Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will … The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me" (Phili 1:15–17). The same outward act, preaching, has opposite inner sources; A depraved mind: "constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1Ti 6:5); Controversies themselves: "foolish, ignorant controversies … breed quarrels" (2Ti 2:23); "avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law" (Tit 3:9).

14280.text: How it co-exists: With envy, often (5 of the 11 verses). Envy is paired with strife in Gal 5:26; Phili 1:15; 1Ti 6:4; 1Cor 3:3 ("jealousy"); in Jam 4:2 it is "covet"; With its named opposites: "that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment" (1Cor 1:10); "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6); "the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone … correcting his opponents with gentleness" (2Ti 2:24–25); "keep in step with the Spirit" (Gal 5:25).

14281.text: What it leads to. Separation from the divider: "avoid them" (Rom 16:17); "after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him … he is self-condemned" (Tit 3:10–11). "You do not have, because you do not ask" (Jam 4:2), so strife blocks asking.

14282.text: Seat. None in-verse: Outside the verse:; Rom 16:18 "deceive the hearts of the naive". Genuine, the victims'; 1Cor 3:1 "spiritual". Not an inner seat of the quarrellers. Not in any batch; Gal 5:24–25 "flesh … Spirit"; 2Ti 2:22 "a pure heart". Genuine. The remedy's site. The seat appears as the remedy (the pure heart, the Spirit) or as the victim (the naive heart). The quarreller's own source is named as passions, flesh or conceit, not as a seat word. This parallels M20 v3 §20 point 2: the seat as the site of the remedy.

14296.text: What it leads to: Understanding (14:29), glory (19:11), and the righteousness that human anger cannot produce: "for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. Therefore put away all filthiness … and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:20–21). Slowness to anger opens the way to receiving the word; A "cool spirit" belongs to the "man of understanding" (Pro 17:27).

14297.text: Seat: In the verse:; Pro 16:32 "spirit" (ruach). The bearer's own, as what is ruled. Genuine; Pro 14:29 "temper" (ruach, "short of spirit"). The bearer's own. Genuine; Outside the verse:; Pro 14:30 "a tranquil heart gives life to the flesh". Genuine; Pro 17:27 "a cool spirit". Genuine; Jam 1:21 "save your souls". Genuine; Across §22 the seat is the ruach, as the thing ruled or kept cool. The anger word and the spirit word stand side by side, and "slow/long" and "short" describe both.

14303.text: Where it comes from. Seeing others prosper: "fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way, over the man who carries out evil devices!" (37:7). Envy is paired with it: "be not envious of wrongdoers" (37:1; Pro 24:19).

14305.text: What it leads to. A reason is given in the next verse, each time: the wicked "will soon fade like the grass" (37:2); "the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land" (37:9); "the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out" (Pro 24:20). The fretting is answered by a longer view of time, which links to §3's anger that has a course: Pro 24:17–18, just before: "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the Lord see it and be displeased". Neither heating oneself at the wicked's success nor rejoicing at their fall is allowed.

14309.text: How it co-exists. Each list faces an opposite: "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience …" (Gal 5:22); "Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (Eph 4:32); "put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge" (Col 3:10); "put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14); In Eph 4:30–31 the list comes straight after "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God". Anger is set as something that grieves the Spirit.

14310.text: Seat. None in-verse: Outside the verse:; Gal 5:19, 22 "flesh … Spirit"; Eph 4:30 "Holy Spirit"; Rom 13:14 "flesh".

14316.text: What it does. It fills, cuts, grinds and cries out: "all in the synagogue were filled with wrath" (Luk 4:28); "they were enraged [literally sawn through] and wanted to kill them" (Act 5:33); "they were enraged [cut to the heart], and they ground their teeth at him" (Act 7:54); "they were enraged and were crying out, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'" (Act 19:28); "Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain?" (Act 4:25, quoting Psa 2).

14317.text: Where it comes from. Hearing: "When they heard these things" (Luk 4:28; Act 5:33; 7:54; 19:28); the grace to the widow of Zarephath and to Naaman rather than to Israel (Luk 4:26–27); "the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him" (Act 5:32); "you who received the law … and did not keep it" (Act 7:53); a threat to trade and to a goddess's standing (Act 19:26–27).

14318.text: How it co-exists: With stopping the ears: "they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Act 7:57). The rage refuses to go on hearing; With a calm figure beside it: "But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God" (Act 7:55). And "passing through their midst, he went away" (Luk 4:30). The seat is again named in the contrast figure; With counsel that restrains it: Gamaliel, "if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" (Act 5:39). They "took his advice", and yet "beat them" (5:40). Restrained from killing, but not from beating.

14319.text: What it leads to: Trying to throw him off a cliff (Luk 4:29), stoning (Act 7:58), a riot (Act 19:29); The end God sets: "all who were incensed against him … shall come and be ashamed" (Isa 45:24); "The nations raged, but your wrath came" (Rev 11:18, B2). The collective rage meets the divine wrath at the end. This is Psa 2 as the apostles read it: "against the Lord and against his Anointed … for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus" (Act 4:26–27).

14320.text: Seat: In the verse:; Act 7:54: the M47 tag's surface is "enraged". The Greek reads dieprionto tais kardiais autōn, "they were sawn through in their hearts" [lexical, not in DB]. The ESV folds "hearts" into "enraged". Genuine. The enraged ones' own heart, as where the word cut. Not in any batch: new; Compare pilot §1.3 (cholaō built on bile) and §1.1 (thumos). Here the seat is a separate word, hidden by the translation, not by the Greek; Act 5:33 uses the same verb without "hearts" [lexical]; Act 4:25 "Holy Spirit". Divine, speaking (the Spirit speaking through David's psalm). Spurious for the ragers; Outside the verse: Act 7:55 "full of the Holy Spirit"; Act 5:32 "the Holy Spirit … given to those who obey". Divine, as received by the other party.

14321.text: What it does to the one attacked: It swallows: "they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us; then the flood would have swept us away" (Psa 124:3–4); It bears a grudge and drops trouble: "they drop trouble upon me, and in anger they bear a grudge against me" (Psa 55:3); It poisons through speech: "They make their tongue sharp as a serpent's, and under their lips is the venom of asps" (140:3); "They have venom like the venom of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear" (58:4). Venom is the image of the enemy's anger in speech. Compare §16's Deu 32:33; In Paul's case it is summed up without detail: "our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn — fighting without and fear within" (2Cor 7:5). Outer conflict and inner fear are named as a pair.

14322.text: Where it comes from. The enemy's heart: "in your hearts you devise wrongs" (Psa 58:2); "who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually" (140:2); they are "estranged from the womb" (58:3).

14323.text: How it co-exists: With the attacked one's inner state named next: "My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me. Fear and trembling come upon me" (Psa 55:4–5). The enemy's anger (55:3) is felt as anguish of heart (55:4); With an appeal to God's anger against it: "Arise, O Lord, in your anger; lift yourself up against the fury of my enemies" (Psa 7:6, B2). The human's answer to another's anger is to call on God's. Compare §24, where the answer to the wicked's success is waiting, not heating oneself.

14324.text: What it leads to. Deliverance, looked back on or asked for: "If it had not been the Lord who was on our side" (Psa 124:1–2); "you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me" (138:7); "all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame" (Isa 41:11), after "fear not, for I am with you" (41:10); "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2Cor 7:6).

14349.text: How it co-exists. The drink comes back to the one who gave it, as God's cup: "You will have your fill of shame instead of glory. Drink, yourself … The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (Hab 2:16); "he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger" (Rev 14:10, divine, read as context).

14350.text: What it does: "let us consider how to stir up [paroxusmos, the word of Act 15:39's 'sharp disagreement'] one another to love and good works" (Heb 10:24); "your zeal has stirred up most of them" (2Cor 9:2); "what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you … what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment!" (2Cor 7:11).

14351.text: Where it comes from: Godly grief: "godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death" (2Cor 7:10). Indignation is one of the fruits of grief that turns toward God; Readiness and zeal (2Cor 9:2); Drawing near "with a true heart" (Heb 10:22).

14353.text: The anger is very often kindled by something perceived: Part 1: thirteen verses name "heard" or "saw" in the verse itself (Gen 34:7; 39:19; Exo 32:19; Judg 9:30; 1Sa 11:6; 17:28; 2Sa 13:21; Neh 4:1, 7; 5:6; Est 3:5; 5:9; Job 32:5); Part 2 adds Psa 112:10; Mat 2:16; 20:24; 21:15; 26:8; Mar 10:14; 10:41; Luk 4:28; Act 5:33; 7:54; 17:16; 19:28; These are counted from the texts cited. No wider count was made.

14354.text: The answer the texts give to human anger is most often a question or a reframing, not a rebuke. This is observed across the passages above, not counted over M02: God's question to Cain (Gen 4:6) and to Jonah (Jon 4:4, 9); Joseph's "not you … but God" (Gen 45:8); the father's "this your brother" (Luk 15:32); Jesus's reframing of the norm for the indignant and of greatness for the rival disciples; Nathan's parable turned round (2Sa 12:7).

14357.text: In-verse seats new to M47: Psa 95:8; Eze 32:9; Act 4:25; 7:54; 16:18; 2Cor 7:5.

14361.text: The frame's words are the seat's substitutes, and nothing here changes that. New: Eph 4:30–31 puts the Spirit's grief directly before the anger list. So the other party affected by human anger is named as the Holy Spirit.

14368.text: (v2) Pro 11:23: Settled as: human (where the wicked's expectation ends) → AL §3; Why: the saying's pair ("the desire of the righteous ends only in good") is about outcomes. Whose wrath the wicked meet is not said. Tentative: it could be God's (unit 2).

14384.text: 2Ch 26:16–21: Sequence the text gives: strength → "he grew proud" (Hebrew his heart was lifted up) → trespass → withstood → anger → leprosy in the act.

14388.text: Job 32:1–20: Sequence the text gives: the friends fall silent → anger ×3 → waiting from deference and fear → "the spirit in man" → belly like wine with no vent → "I must speak, that I may find relief".

14389.text: (v2) Psa 37:1–9: Sequence the text gives: seeing the wicked prosper → heating oneself (fret) + envy → "trust … commit … be still … wait" → "refrain from anger" → the wicked fade, the waiting inherit.

14390.text: (v2) Psa 55:3–5: Sequence the text gives: the enemy's noise → their anger bears a grudge → "my heart is in anguish within me" → terrors of death → fear and trembling.

14400.text: (v2) Act 7:53–58: Sequence the text gives: accusation heard → sawn through in their hearts → teeth ground → Stephen full of the Spirit sees glory → they stop their ears → rush, cast out, stone.

14416.text: (v2) Pro 16:32: Seat word (Strong's as tagged): "spirit" ruach (H7307G); Phenomenon: SL §22; Whose seat: the bearer's own, as what is ruled; Seat-sense check: genuine; Already read in: A v3 §2.1 [H]; H v1 §1.5; C v3 §1.6.

14498.text: Part B: Psa 106:32. "They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psa 106:32–33): The psalm gives an inner route for the "because of you" that Moses spoke of in Deuteronomy. The people's provocation reaches a spirit, and Moses' rash speech follows; Whose spirit is not determinable. The M47 spirit classification v2 marks Psa 106:33 as [U] (#1880 item C-R4; C v3 R4). It could be Moses' spirit embittered, or God's Spirit rebelled against (compare Isa 63:10). Either way, the verse ties Meribah to Moses' loss "on their account".

14502.text: Part B: Psa 7:11; 18:7; 21:9; 78:49; 78:50; 110:5; Isa 30:27; 30:30; 66:14; 66:15: Psa 18:7 is the psalm text of 2Sa 22:8: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … because he was angry" (Psa 18:6–7); The upright in heart, and the call to repent. "God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day" (Psa 7:11). This follows "you who test the minds and hearts … who saves the upright in heart" (7:9–10), and is followed by "If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword" (7:12). The protection is for the upright in heart, and the indignation waits on repentance; The king who trusts: "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5); The Exodus retold: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psa 78:50). "Then he led out his people like sheep" (78:52); The protected rejoice in the heart; "You shall have a song … and gladness of heart" (Isa 30:29), while "the Assyrians will be terror-stricken" (30:31); "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you … You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass" (66:13–14); The protected are the people the anger struck earlier: "the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26); Seat ; In the verse: Isa 66:14 "your heart shall rejoice". The comforted people's own. Genuine. Psa 78:50 "them" (nephesh) is the Egyptians' life. Life-sense; Outside: Psa 7:9–10 "hearts" / "upright in heart". Isa 30:29 "gladness of heart"; What part B adds. Part A had only praise (Exo 15). Part B places the joy of the protected in the heart.

14503.text: Part C: Eze 36:6; Nah 1:2; Hab 3:8; 3:12; Zec 8:2: Anger for the reproached: "Behold, I have spoken in my jealous wrath, because you have suffered the reproach of the nations" (Eze 36:6). Edom took the land "with wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (36:5). "you will soon come home" (36:8); "I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath. … I have returned to Zion" (Zec 8:2–3). "The Lord … keeps wrath for his enemies" (Nah 1:2); Habakkuk's prayer, from inside the fear:; "O Lord, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O Lord, do I fear … in wrath remember mercy" (Hab 3:2); "Was your wrath against the rivers …? … You went out for the salvation of your people" (3:8, 13); the enemy came "rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret" (3:14); then: "I hear, and my body trembles; my lips quiver … rottenness enters into my bones … Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us" (3:16); and: "Though the fig tree should not blossom … yet I will rejoice in the Lord" (3:17–18).

14507.text: What it leads to. The people are spared. In Deuteronomy, the memory of the intercession is itself turned into instruction (Deu 9:25–29, "So I lay prostrate …"), set against the people's claim to righteousness.

14508.text: Seat: In the verse: Num 16:22 "spirits of all flesh". God's relation to every human spirit, given as the ground of the plea. Genuine. Nothing new; Outside: none in Exo 32:7–15; Deu 9:15–22; Pointer: the fasting body (Deu 9:18) does the seat's work here, as the face and bed do in U1 §1.

14509.text: Part B: Psa 106:23. "Therefore he said he would destroy them — had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them.": The psalm names Moses' intercession (Exo 32; Deu 9) "standing in the breach". Its context is "They forgot God, their Savior" (106:21); Part B also shows intercession forbidden and absent:; forbidden: "As for you, do not pray for this people … do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you"; absent: "there was no one to intercede"; repaid with evil: Jer 18:20.

14510.text: Part C: Eze 9:8; Dan 9:16; Zec 1:12: The prophet refused. "while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, 'Ah, Lord God! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel …?'" (Eze 9:8). The answer is no: "The guilt … is exceedingly great … For they say, 'The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see.' As for me, my eye will not spare" (9:9–10). Some are spared: the mark is put "on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations" (9:4, context read). Those who grieve over the sin are marked. The one who pleads for the rest is not answered; Daniel's confession-intercession:; "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem … because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem … [has] become a byword" (Dan 9:16); "the Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (9:14); "for your own sake" (9:17); "we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy" (9:18); An angel intercedes: "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem …, against which you have been angry these seventy years?" This is answered with "gracious and comforting words" (Zec 1:12–13).

14515.text: Part B: Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8. Three more uses of the name. Pilot §2.2 already lists all three as uses of the idiom: An individual's plea against "insolent men": "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger … Turn to me and be gracious to me" (Psa 86:14–16); A recital with its reasoning: "He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins" (103:9–10). This comes straight after "He made known his ways to Moses" (103:7). The psalm names Moses as the one to whom the name was made known; Praise: "The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made" (145:9); The one creed is now used five ways: worship (Exo 34:8), plea (Num 14; Psa 86), confession (Neh 9), complaint and praise (Psa 145); Seat . Outside: Psa 86:13 "you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol". The pleader's own. Genuine.

14520.text: Part C: Eze 43:8. "setting their threshold by my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, with only a wall between me and them. They have defiled my holy name … so I have consumed them in my anger." Then: "Now let them put away their whoring … and I will dwell in their midst forever" (43:9), and the temple is to be described "that they may be ashamed of their iniquities" (43:10): Part A's nearness was a danger of approach (Uzzah). Here the nearness is profaned by building one's own house against God's. The remedy is a new dwelling and shame.

14526.text: Part B: Psa 78:58, 78:59, 78:62; Isa 65:3; Jer 7:18, 7:19, 7:20; 11:17; 15:14; 17:4; 25:6, 25:7; 32:29, 32:30, 32:31, 32:32 (16 verses): More roots; Treachery like the fathers': "turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow" (Psa 78:57); Self-holiness: "who say, 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you'" (Isa 65:5). This is said to a God who says "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2); Trust in man: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the Lord" (Jer 17:5); From youth, turning the back: "done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth" (Jer 32:30); "They have turned to me their back and not their face … they have not listened to receive instruction" (32:33); Whole households, all ranks: "The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough … to provoke me to anger" (Jer 7:18); "their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets" (32:32); The provocation turns on the provoker. "Is it I whom they provoke? declares the Lord. Is it not themselves, to their own shame?" (Jer 7:19); "that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm" (25:7); Pilot §2 lists Jer 7 in the ka'as series; What part B adds is the text's own statement that the provoking harms the provoker. Part A had "they … became false" (2Ki 17:15). Jeremiah adds "to their own shame" and "to your own harm"; Seat . Outside: Jer 17:5 "whose heart turns away". Genuine. Nothing new.

14530.text: How it co-exists: The provocation is inherited. "you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the Lord" (Num 32:14). The sons are warned that they are repeating the fathers. They answer by offering to go armed before their brothers (32:16–17); Remembering is commanded against self-righteousness. "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (Deu 9:4); "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath in the wilderness" (9:7). Memory of provoking God is the cure for the heart's claim to righteousness; Moses caught between. In Num 11:10–15 Moses hears the weeping, is "displeased", and says: "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? … kill me at once … that I may not see my wretchedness" (11:11, 15). The leader between God's anger and the people's complaint asks to die.

14532.text: Seat: In the verse: Num 11:33 "meat" (basar). Spurious. Pilot §0 lists it among the links that do not count; Outside: Num 32:7, 9 "discourage the heart of the people". The people's own heart, as what the spies weakened. Genuine. Deu 9:4–5 "Do not say in your heart … the uprightness of your heart". Genuine. Num 32:7, 9 is not cited in any batch. New as an M02 context seat: discouraging the heart of others is what provokes the anger.

14541.text: Part B: Psa 106:29. "Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed. And that was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever" (106:30–31). The psalm adds the verdict on the act: it was counted as righteousness.

14550.text: Part C: Eze 36:18. "I poured out my wrath upon them … I scattered them among the nations." Then: "wherever they came, they profaned my holy name, in that people said of them, 'These are the people of the Lord, and yet they had to go out of his land'" (36:18–20): The nations read the exile as a failure of God. This is the reverse of Deu 29:24–25, where the nations read it rightly; The exiles, simply by being exiles, give the wrong reading.

14551.text: What it does. "Give to Levi your Thummim … whom you tested at Massah, with whom you quarreled at the waters of Meribah" (Deu 33:8).

14554.text: U1 §12 reads Meribah as human contention with God that costs the leaders the land. Deu 33:8 adds a second reading: at the same place, one party was "godly" and was found faithful by testing.

14555.text: Part B: Psa 81:7. "In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah." Then: "O Israel, if you would but listen to me!" (81:8): A second text reads Meribah as God's test (with Deu 33:8). Here the test stands beside a deliverance, and is recalled to call Israel to listen.

14574.text: What it does: Foreseen in Solomon's prayer: "If they sin against you — for there is no one who does not sin — and you are angry with them … yet if they turn their heart … and repent … with all their heart and with all their soul … then hear" (1Ki 8:46–49; 2Ch 6:36–39); Josiah hears the book: "he tore his clothes … 'great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not obeyed'" (2Ki 22:11, 13; 2Ch 34:19, 21). The answer names the heart: "because your heart was penitent [tender], and you humbled yourself … and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you" (2Ki 22:19; 2Ch 34:27); Rehoboam and the princes: "humbled themselves and said, 'The Lord is righteous.' When the Lord saw that they humbled themselves … I will not destroy them" (2Ch 12:6–7); "when he humbled himself the wrath of the Lord turned from him" (12:12); Hezekiah's pride and humbling: "Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came … But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah" (2Ch 32:25–26); Ezra confesses: "you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved … shall we break your commandments again …? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us …? … you are just … none can stand before you" (Ezr 9:13–15); Manasseh: "when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the Lord his God and humbled himself greatly … Then Manasseh knew that the Lord was God" (2Ch 33:12–13).

14576.text: How it co-exists: Humbling with a confession of God's justice: "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); "you are just" (Ezr 9:15); Humbling with the body: torn clothes and weeping (Josiah); Humbling that is partial. Rehoboam is spared destruction but made to serve Shishak, "that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms" (2Ch 12:8). Bronze shields replace gold (12:10). And "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (12:14). The humbling turned the wrath, and the heart was still not set.

14578.text: Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 32:25 "his heart was proud" and 32:26 "the pride of his heart". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; D v2 §9.1, §10.1, §11; pilot §2; Outside (all genuine, the bearer's own):; 1Ki 8:47–48 / 2Ch 6:37–38 "turn their heart … with all their heart and with all their soul"; 2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27 "your heart was penitent / tender"; 2Ch 12:14 "did not set his heart to seek the Lord"; Nothing new in any single seat. What part A adds is a third kind of seat for pilot §2. The pilot has the heart that provokes (the cause) and the spirit that receives (the effect). Part A adds the heart that turns, and so turns the anger away. In these verses, and in §22, it is the human seat most often named in the context of God's anger. For the researcher: whether pilot §2 takes this as a third row.

14589.text: What it does: Removal: Josiah "removed all the shrines … which kings of Israel had made, provoking the Lord to anger" (2Ki 23:19); Covenant formed in the heart: "Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord … in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us. My sons, do not now be negligent" (2Ch 29:10–11); A call to return: "Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the Lord … that his fierce anger may turn away from you. For if you return … your brothers and your children will find compassion" (2Ch 30:8–9); Separation: "Let our officials stand for the whole assembly … until the fierce wrath of our God over this matter is turned away from us" (Ezr 10:14); Sabbath restored: "Now you are bringing more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath" (Neh 13:18), then the gates are shut (13:19); Captives released:; Oded: "you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven … Have you not sins of your own against the Lord your God? … send back the captives … for the fierce wrath of the Lord is upon you" (2Ch 28:9–11); The chiefs: "you propose to bring upon us guilt against the Lord in addition to our present sins … there is fierce wrath against Israel" (28:13); Then: "with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them … provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk" (28:15). Fear of adding to the wrath turns into care for enemies who are also kin; Rebuke acted on: "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you … Nevertheless, some good is found in you … you … have set your heart to seek God" (2Ch 19:2–3). Jehoshaphat "went out again among the people … and brought them back to the Lord" (19:4).

14590.text: Where it comes from: From reading the ruin; From a prophet's word (2Ch 19:2; 28:9); From awareness of accumulated guilt ("our guilt is already great", 2Ch 28:13; "we have greatly transgressed", Ezr 10:13); From the fathers' example as a warning ("Did not your fathers act in this way …?", Neh 13:18; "Do not be like your fathers", 2Ch 30:7).

14603.text: What it does: Eliphaz: "who that was innocent ever perished? … those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed" (Job 4:7–9); Zophar: "To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body" (20:23); "dragged off in the day of God's wrath. This is the wicked man's portion" (20:28–29); Job contests it from what he has seen: "How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? … That God distributes pains in his anger?" (21:17); "Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath" (21:20). He also cites travellers' testimony "that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath" (21:29–30); Elihu: "because his anger does not punish … Job opens his mouth in empty talk" (35:15–16); God: "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (42:7).

14630.text: What it leads to: song (Psa 30:4); trust; "With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation" (Isa 12:3); a new heart given (Jer 32:39).

14634.text: Where it comes from. From the ruin, seen and suffered: the taunts of neighbours (79:4; 80:6); the sanctuary destroyed (74:3); the king's crown "in the dust" (89:39); "Our holy and beautiful house … has been burned by fire" (Isa 64:11).

14635.text: How it co-exists: Past mercy as the ground: "You forgave the iniquity of your people … You withdrew all your wrath … Restore us again" (Psa 85:2–4); "Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?" (85:6); Relationship as the ground:; "the sheep of your pasture" (74:1); "Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old" (74:2); "you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand … please look, we are all your people" (Isa 64:8–9); Confession, or none; Isa 64 confesses: "you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved? … all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment" (64:5–6); Psa 79 asks: "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Psa 89 does not confess. It holds God to his covenant (89:38–39); The anger reaches even prayer:; "angry with your people's prayers" (Psa 80:4); "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7).

14646.text: What it leads to: Healing: "I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will lead him and restore comfort to him and his mourners" (Isa 57:18); God dwelling with the contrite: "I dwell … with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (57:15).

14647.text: Seat: In the verse:; Isa 57:16 "spirit". The human spirit, as what would faint. Genuine; Isa 57:17 "his own heart". The backslider's. Genuine; Outside: Psa 78:37 "heart"; 78:39 "flesh … wind"; Isa 57:15. Nothing new.

14648.text: Part C: Eze 20:8; 20:13; 20:21; Hos 11:9: Three times in one chapter: "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them … But I acted for the sake of my name" (Eze 20:8–9, 13–14, 21–22: "I withheld my hand"). The chapter ends: "you shall remember your ways … and you shall loathe yourselves … when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways" (20:43–44); Hosea gives another reason: "How can I give you up, O Ephraim? … My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hos 11:8–9). The people were "bent on turning away from me" (11:7). They will return "trembling like birds from Egypt" (11:11); The reasons given for restraint now include God's own nature ("God and not a man"), beside human frailty and the name; What the restrained do:; they remember and loathe themselves (Eze 20:43; also 16:63: "that you may remember and be confounded … when I atone for you"); they come trembling (Hos 11:10–11); Seat . Outside: Hos 11:8 "My heart recoils". God's. Divine.

14654.text: What it does: "Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death" (Pro 11:4); "The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it" (22:14); "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him" (24:17–18); "Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?" (Ecc 5:6).

14659.text: How it co-exists: The people consume themselves: "no one spares another. They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry … each devours the flesh of his own arm, Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh" (Isa 9:19–21); Futility: "They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing" (Jer 12:13); Wealth is no refuge: "What will you do on the day of punishment …? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth?".

14662.text: Part C: Zep 3:8; Zec 7:12; Mal 1:4: Correction refused: "I said, 'Surely you will fear me; you will accept correction' … But all the more they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt" (Zep 3:7). The next verse (3:8) is wrath on the nations, followed by "a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the Lord" (3:9); The heart made hard against hearing: "they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears … They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came" (Zec 7:11–12); Refusal returned in kind: "As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear" (7:13); Rebuilding against the blow, again: "If Edom says, 'We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins,' the Lord of hosts says, 'They may build, but I will tear down … the people with whom the Lord is angry forever'" (Mal 1:4). This is Isa 9:10's "we will build with dressed stones" said by another nation; Seat . In the verse: Zec 7:12 "hearts diamond-hard". The people's own. Genuine. The same verse has "his Spirit" (God's; divine). Outside: Zec 7:10 "devise evil against another in your heart"; What part C adds. Part B's "heart that does not take it in" was a failure to understand. Zec 7:12 names an act: the heart made hard so as not to hear.

14671.text: Where it comes from: Pride: "I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless" (Isa 13:11); Exulting over plunder: "Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage" (Jer 50:11).

They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces" (7:17–18); Survivors "moaning, each one over his iniquity" (7:16); Wealth useless: "Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the Lord. For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people" (Luk 21:23), with "let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains" (21:21); Seat ; In the verse: Eze 7:19 "hunger" (nephesh). The people's appetite. Appetite-sense; Outside: Eze 21:15 "that their hearts may melt". Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

14680.text: Part C: Zep 2:2; 2:3; Rev 6:16: Hiding offered, with "perhaps": "Gather together, yes, gather, O shameless nation, before the decree takes effect … Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land … seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:1–3). The way to be hidden is seeking, humility and righteousness, and even then only "perhaps"; Hiding from God, not in him: "the kings of the earth and the great ones … and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb'" (Rev 6:15–16); This is the reverse of Isa 26:20.
