14966.text: The passage. The Rabshakeh's speech has been heard (2Ki 18). Hezekiah "tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the Lord" (19:1). His message: "This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace" (19:3). Isaiah answers: "Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me" (19:6). A letter comes; Hezekiah "spread it before the Lord" and prays (19:14–19). The Lord answers with an oracle against Sennacherib (19:21–28), and the camp is struck (19:35). 2Ch 32 tells the same campaign with the purpose of the shouting stated (32:18) and the end: "he returned with shame of face to his own land" (32:21).

14975.text: Sennacherib as a passage. Mockery of God sent through servants, letters and shouting; its stated aim is to make the hearers afraid (2Ch 32:18). Hezekiah's response: sackcloth, the house of the Lord, the letter spread before God, prayer (2Ki 19:1, 14–19). God's word to the people: "Do not be afraid" (19:6). God names himself as the one mocked (19:22), knows the mocker's raging (19:27), turns the scorn back (19:21), and the mocker goes home with shame of face (2Ch 32:21). Hezekiah calls the day one "of disgrace" (2Ki 19:3, a contempt word, M06).

15002.text: The original: "it is a disgrace" uses ḥeseḏ (H2617B), the homonym of the word for steadfast love. The lexicon gives this one sense, "shame", in two verses (here and Pro 14:34).

15004.text: mocking carried by a boast from a lifted-up stance (2Ki 19:22–23).

15036.text: The passage. Goliath challenges the ranks of Israel (17:8–10), and Saul and Israel are "dismayed and greatly afraid" (17:11). Every morning and evening for forty days (17:16) the same words, and "All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid" (17:24). David hears (17:23), asks (17:26), is rebuked by Eliab (17:28; told in 10.15), tells Saul "Let no man's heart fail because of him" (17:32), and goes out "in the name of the Lord of hosts" (17:45).

15047.text: The passage. Rachel "saw that she bore Jacob no children, she envied her sister", and said, "Give me children, or I shall die!" (30:1). Jacob's anger is kindled: "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?" (30:2). Then "God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb" (30:22).

15048.text: What the passage carries: the reproach had an inner side before it was removed: envy of her sister and "or I shall die" (30:1). It was felt as a matter of life and death. Jacob answers with anger and with "Am I in the place of God …?" (30:2). God's remembering and listening (30:22) come before the removal.

15053.text: The passage: "We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up" (15:1–2). Then 15:3. Then "whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope" (15:4).

15064.text: M80 Blessing (16) is the curse words beside blessing (Deu 11, 27–30). M19 Trust & Refuge (19) is the pairing of trust and not being put to shame (for example Psa 25:2, 20; 31:1; Rom 5:5 is in the claims register).

15071.text: H2617B ḥeseḏ: the homonym of the word for steadfast love, here "disgrace" (Lev 20:17) and "reproach" (Pro 14:34).

15085.text: Its removal is a gift. "I will remove from your midst your proudly exultant ones, and you shall no longer be haughty in my holy mountain. But I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly" (Zep 3:11–12).

15087.text: These verses join pride to the turning away from God: Pride is a witness against its owner. "The pride of Israel testifies to his face; yet they do not return to the Lord their God, nor seek him, for all this" (Hos 7:10; also Hos 5:5); It goes with not knowing. The verse before says "Strangers devour his strength, and he knows it not; gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, and he knows it not" (Hos 7:9). In Hos 5:4–5, "they know not the Lord" stands next to "The pride of Israel testifies to his face"; Pride does not listen; "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15). The opposite of pride here is hearing; Then: "if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride" (13:17); The pride God will "spoil" belongs to a people "who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart" (13:9–10); Pride leaves a cry unanswered; "There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men" (Job 35:12); The cry has no turning to God in it: "none says, 'Where is God my Maker'" (35:10); I read: this cry is a cry of pain that does not seek God; God works to keep pride from a man. He speaks "in a dream ... that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man; he keeps back his soul from the pit" (Job 33:15–18). God's warning is aimed at pride before it ripens; The wicked does not see. "If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness ... and does not see the majesty of the Lord" (Isa 26:10). Not seeing God's majesty sits in the same verse as not learning from his favour.

15088.text: In these verses pride is not alone. It stands over someone weaker or someone righteous: The poor:; "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor" (Psa 10:2); Sodom's guilt was "pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy" (Eze 16:49). Pride is listed with plenty and ease, and with what was not done for others; The widow: "The Lord tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries" (Pro 15:25). Pride's house is set against the boundary of the one without defence; The righteous:; Lips "which speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt" (Psa 31:18); "The arrogant have hidden a trap for me" (Psa 140:5); "Let not the foot of arrogance come upon me" (Psa 36:11). Pride is pictured as a foot that treads; The heart closed to pity. "They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly" (Psa 17:10). A closed heart and an arrogant mouth sit side by side; The one who bears it; "Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud" (Psa 123:4); The psalm's answer is the eyes of a servant looking to the master's hand "till he has mercy upon us" (123:2); This is pride as it is felt by the one under it; Another's fall in one's mouth. "Was not your sister Sodom a byword in your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was uncovered?" (Eze 16:56–57). In the day of its pride, Jerusalem talked of Sodom's fall while its own wickedness was still covered; Taunting God's people. Moab and Ammon's lot comes "in return for their pride, because they taunted and boasted against the people of the Lord" (Zep 2:10); Repaid. "repay to the proud what they deserve" (Psa 94:2). The proud "pour out their arrogant words" and "crush your people" (94:4–5). "The Lord preserves the faithful but abundantly repays the one who acts in pride" (Psa 31:23). "let them be trapped in their pride" (Psa 59:12); Carried from M09: Isa 13:11 ("the pomp of the arrogant") and Job 22:29.

15089.text: Here the word names a thing more than a bearing: what a people stands on: Might; "the pride of your power" (Lev 26:19); Egypt's "proud might" (Eze 30:6, 18) and Israel's "proud might" (Eze 33:28), whose people "rely on the sword" (33:26); "the pride of the strong" (Eze 7:24); Splendour and pomp; Babylon, "the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans" (Isa 13:19); Tyre: "to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth" (Isa 23:9); "the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim ... the fading flower of its glorious beauty" (Isa 28:1, 3); Strongholds. "I abhor the pride of Jacob and hate his strongholds" (Amo 6:8). In the passage they lie at ease and are "not grieved over the ruin of Joseph" (6:6); What God gave, used for pride; "His beautiful ornament they used for pride, and they made their abominable images and their detestable things of it" (Eze 7:20); "Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul" (Eze 24:21). God's own sanctuary had become what they gloried in. It sits with delight and yearning: a pride, a delight and a longing all set on one thing; Brought down; "Your pomp is brought down to Sheol" (Isa 14:11). The passage names the heart behind it: "You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven ... I will set my throne on high'" (14:13); The pride of Egypt (Eze 32:12), Assyria (Zec 10:11) and Philistia (Zec 9:6); Carried from M09 (the proud brought low): Isa 25:11, Isa 2:12, Dan 4:37, Job 40:11–12.

15099.text: The challenge to Job: "Adorn yourself with majesty and dignity; clothe yourself with glory and splendor. Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him ... Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you" (Job 40:10–14); Majesty is joined to what only God does: abasing every proud one, and saving by his own hand.

15109.text: What the batch 1 verses state: The same words are used of God and of people. gāʾôn, gaʾăwāh, gēʾût and gāʾāh name God's majesty (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10) and human pride (Isa 9:9; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18). So yes: these words describe a characteristic of God. In ESV English the difference shows in the choice of word ("majesty" against "pride"), not in the Hebrew; God's majesty is his own and is not taken on. He is "robed in majesty" while "you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). Nothing in these verses shows it being acquired. It is shown in acts: the sea, the overthrow, the thunder; It is challenged, but it is not overturned. The researcher's word "undisputed" needs one qualification from the verses. God's majesty is disputed: by the enemy at the sea (Exo 15:9), by "all that is proud and lofty" (Isa 2:12), and by the one who says "I will ascend to heaven" (Isa 14:13). Each time the dispute ends with the one who rose brought down. So it is not uncontested; it is never overturned; Majesty goes with what only God can do. Job 40:10–14 makes the test plain: whoever wears majesty must abase every proud one and save by his own hand. Only God does; Human pride in these verses is mostly a standing that is taken, or kept against God; It is said in the heart against the facts: "the bricks have fallen, but we will build" (Isa 9:10); It is worn as a show (Psa 73:6); It is set over the weak (Psa 10:2; Eze 16:49; Pro 15:25); It refuses to hear (Jer 13:15–17); It stands on might and strongholds (Lev 26:19; Amo 6:8; Eze 33:26); This agrees with the researcher's "mostly assumed"; But the same word for people is not always assumed. God gives a "pride" to his people: chosen (Psa 47:4), given (Isa 4:2), made (Isa 60:15), restored (Nah 2:2). The Lord himself is their "triumph" (Deu 33:29). The verses also show a given honour turned into pride (Eze 7:20; 24:21); I read: the line the verses draw is not between God having majesty and people having none. It runs between a standing that is one's own by nature (God), a standing given by God (his people), and a standing taken, or turned against the giver (pride); The Son's majesty is described as received, and it stands beside his being handed over; "he received honor and glory from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17); "after making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty" (Heb 1:3); At the very moment of "the majesty of God", he speaks of being "delivered into the hands of men" (Luk 9:43–44); This joins 13.1 Lowering himself (M09): the one with majesty did not hold onto it in the way pride holds; I read: where Php 2:6–9 joins the two, it lies outside this batch's words; A majesty that depends on people is the contrast. Artemis's "magnificence" can be "deposed", because it rests on "she whom all Asia and the world worship" (Act 19:27). I read: this is the borrowed standing that pride is, set against God's majesty, which no one confers.

15111.text: Pride over the poor and the widow (Psa 10:2; Eze 16:49; Pro 15:25) bears on OT-105 (the poor as seen by another).

15112.text: The M72 forward mark Psa 36:11, "the foot of arrogance", is read here (group III).

15117.text: It has no room for God: "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psa 10:4); "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4). Then: "an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol" (2:5). The swollen soul is set against faith, and joined to restlessness and greed.

15118.text: It is seen in the eyes, the walk and the house: "Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin" (Pro 21:4). It follows "the Lord weighs the heart" (21:2); "Whoever has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure" (Psa 101:5); The daughters of Zion "walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes" (Isa 3:16), in the same oracle as "the spoil of the poor is in your houses" (3:14); "he who makes his door high seeks destruction" (Pro 17:19); "How sick is your heart ... the deeds of a brazen prostitute" (Eze 16:30).

15132.text: The eyes lifted against the Holy One. "Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel!" (2Ki 19:22; Isa 37:23).

15136.text: Ripening and fall: "the rod has blossomed; pride has budded" (Eze 7:10). Pride is pictured as a plant that has come to bud; "all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble", while "for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing" (Mal 4:1–2); The fallen cedar is made an example: "in order that no trees by the waters may grow to towering height ... For they are all given over to death" (Eze 31:14); Shebna, who "cut out a tomb on the height", is hurled away: "you shame of your master's house" (Isa 22:16–18).

15146.text: The verses say outright that pride takes a place that is God's: "you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods' ... yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "Who will bring me down to the ground?" (Obd 3); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); This is the researcher's "assumed position" in the verses' own words. Pride is a heart made like the heart of a god. It is not so; What was given is turned into pride; "the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar ... kingship and greatness and glory and majesty ... But when his heart was lifted up" (Dan 5:18–20). Majesty is the same word family God wears (batch 1); The pattern recurs: Uzziah's strength (2Ch 26:15–16), Hezekiah's healing (2Ch 32:24–25), the cherub's beauty (Eze 28:17), the cedar's height (Eze 31:9–10); I read: the human standing in these verses is real, and it is given. Pride begins when the heart treats it as its own. Batch 1 showed the same in Eze 7:20 and 24:21; God's height does not keep him from the low. "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psa 138:6). The high God comes near the lowly. The proud, who make themselves high, are known "from afar"; Lifting up belongs to God. "not from the east or from the west ... comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:6–7). The one who has height by nature is the one who gives height; God is known as greater through his answer to arrogance. "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods, because ... they dealt arrogantly" (Exo 18:11). "you knew that they acted arrogantly ... And you made a name for yourself" (Neh 9:10); God knows and weighs. "Talk no more so very proudly ... for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1Sa 2:3). This is joined to "the Lord weighs the heart" (Pro 21:2) beside "a proud heart" (21:4). I read: pride claims a height that cannot bear being weighed. God's knowing is part of what it runs into; His mercy answers presumption. "they acted presumptuously ... But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful" (Neh 9:16–17). "insolent men have risen up against me ... But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (Psa 86:14–15).

15151.text: The Greek picture is swelling, physioō, "to inflate". In Paul it is set again and again against love: Knowledge. "This 'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Co 8:1–3). Swelling knowledge is answered not by more knowledge but by being known by God; Love is not. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4). Before this: "if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge ... but have not love, I am nothing" (13:2); Party; "that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:6–7); Here Paul states what the Hebrew verses showed in story: pride holds what was received "as if you did not receive it"; Talk without power. "Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you ... I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power" (1Co 4:18–20). The arrogance rests on Paul being absent; Where grief belongs. "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1Co 5:2). Pride stands where mourning should be; Without reason. "puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head" (Col 2:18–19, carried from M09); The new convert. "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6). The verse joins conceit to the devil's condemnation. It does not say what the devil's condemnation was. I read: it is held for 13.3 (other spirits). It is not built on here; Controversy. "he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension" (1Ti 6:4). Conceit is joined to understanding nothing, and to quarrels; With pleasure. "swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2Ti 3:4–5); Among the others; "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Co 12:20); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26), after "let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (5:25); Conceit is named among the things that set people against each other.

15158.text: From within. "from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts ... coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person" (Mar 7:21–23). Jesus places pride in the heart.

15160.text: Love turned inward. "lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant", ending "lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God" (2Ti 3:2–4). The list begins and ends with what is loved.

15179.text: Evil and desire: "Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day" (Psa 52:1). The boast is answered by God's steadfast love; "the wicked boasts of the desires of his soul" (Psa 10:3). This is the verse before "In the pride of his face" (10:4, batch 2).

15195.text: The boast is not removed. It is moved: The command. "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17). This follows Christ "who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1:30). It is joined to "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends" (2Co 10:18); What to boast in; "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24); The boast is in knowing God, and what is known is his character; The soul's boast. "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2, carried); Not in my bow. "For not in my bow do I trust ... In God we have boasted continually" (Psa 44:6–8). The psalm then turns: "But you have rejected us" (44:9). The boast in God is kept in the psalm even while the defeat is brought before him; His name. "Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!" (Psa 105:3; 1Ch 16:10); The worm. "Fear not, you worm Jacob ... you shall rejoice in the Lord; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory" (Isa 41:14–16). The one called a worm is the one who glories; Justified and glorying. "Only in the Lord, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength ... In the Lord all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory" (Isa 45:24–25); The nations. If Israel returns and swears in truth, "nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory" (Jer 4:2); Exulting; "all who swear by him shall exult" (Psa 63:11); "Let the righteous one rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!" (Psa 64:10); "that I may glory with your inheritance" (Psa 106:5); The cross. "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Gal 6:14); Christ, not the flesh. "glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh — though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Php 3:3–4). Paul has standing in the flesh, "I have more", and sets it aside; Hope, sufferings, God. ESV renders kauchaomai "rejoice" here:; "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Rom 5:2–3); "we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (5:11); The same word that elsewhere is a proud boast is here joy in hope, in suffering, and in God; Held fast. "if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope" (Heb 3:6); The conscience. "our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12). The boast is a clear conscience, and its ground is named as grace.

15199.text: God is not the subject of a boast in these verses. He is its right object, and his character is what is boasted in. "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24). The proper boast is knowing God as he is: The boast is moved, not removed. The same impulse that boasts in wisdom, might and riches (Jer 9:23) is turned to God (9:24; 1Co 1:31). It becomes joy in hope and in suffering (Rom 5:2–3); I read: set beside batches 1–3, the human "lifting" is not abolished. Where it rests on oneself it is pride. Where it rests on God it is glory in him. This fits Ch 12 claim C-182 (the boast moved to what God does). It is a reconciliation point when that chapter is touched; Gift excludes self-boasting. "it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Eph 2:8–9). "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1Co 4:7). "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Gal 6:3); This is the researcher's "assumed" in the verses' words: a standing held as one's own when it was received, or thought when it is not so; The contrast with God, from batches 1–3, is that his standing is neither received nor assumed; The measure is assigned. "the area of influence God assigned to us" (2Co 10:13), and in batch 3 "the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). I read: where God's height is his by nature, a person's rightful standing is a measure given, and pride boasts "beyond limits"; Christ's power in weakness. "my power is made perfect in weakness ... so that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2Co 12:9). The boast in weakness makes room for another's power. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself, as in batch 3 §3.4; God's steadfast love answers the boast of evil. "Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day" (Psa 52:1). God's character is set over the mighty man's boast, as his mercy answered presumption in batch 2 §3.7.

15200.text: Boasting is the speech of pride, and it can be redeemed. One account should hold both sides: the boast in self (I) and the boast in the Lord (III). Splitting them would lose the turn that Jer 9:23–24 and 1Co 1:31 make.

15205.text: Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). Again the opposite of scoffing is hearing; "the scoffer cease ... who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate" (Isa 29:20–21). The scoffer works against the one who reproves. In the same passage "The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord" (29:19); Wine and company; "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" (Pro 20:1); "the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers", and "none of them calls upon me" (Hos 7:5, 7); In Job's debates; Zophar: "when you mock, shall no one shame you?" (Job 11:3); Job: "after I have spoken, mock on" (21:3); Elihu: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (36:18); I read: the charge of scoffing is thrown between the speakers. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.

15228.text: "The kings of the earth set themselves ... against the Lord and against his Anointed ... He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision" (Psa 2:2–4). Then: "As for me, I have set my King on Zion" (2:6).

15232.text: If they turn to other gods, "Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples" (1Ki 9:7; 2Ch 7:20; Deu 28:37). "a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (Jer 24:9). "a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror" (Eze 5:15).

15238.text: The scoffer and hearing: the scoffer's mark is refusing rebuke (Pro 13:1; 15:12; 9:7–8). With batch 1 (Jer 13:15) and batch 2 (Pro 13:10), the M08 words keep setting pride against hearing. This bears on 10.2 Humility and hearing.

15243.text: Pride sense (42). These include: the heart proud or haughty: 2Ch 32:25–26; 2Ch 26:16; Eze 28:2, 5, 17; Eze 31:10; Pro 16:5; Pro 18:12; Psa 101:5; a haughty spirit: Pro 16:18; Ecc 7:8; haughty eyes and looks: Isa 5:15; 2Ki 19:22 and Isa 37:23 (lifting the eyes against the Holy One); the lofty brought low: Isa 10:33; Isa 26:5; Eze 31:14; "do not become proud, but fear": Rom 11:20; Rom 12:16, 2Co 10:5 ("every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God") and Luk 16:15; Obd 3–4 and Jer 49:16 (the nest set high); Isa 3:16 (the daughters of Zion) and Isa 22:16 (Shebna's tomb on the height). These two have no other M-code.

15245.text: Two of these bear on Jesus, and so on 13.1 (#2148): Isa 52:13 (the servant "high and lifted up") and Heb 7:26 (a high priest "exalted above the heavens").

15247.text: The overview's surface pointer was a surface match only. The reading gives 42 pride-sense verses. Some surfaces such as "exalted" turned out to be God's or another's raising, so they are S or D (Isa 5:16, Isa 52:13, 2Ch 7:21, Act 13:17). Some plain surfaces such as "high" carry pride (Pro 17:19 "makes his door high", Psa 75:5, Isa 22:16).

15248.text: M09 humility: Verses: Isa 57:15, Jam 1:9, Eze 17:24, Eze 21:26, Job 5:11, Ecc 5:8.

15249.text: M12 righteousness: Verses: Psa 10:5, Isa 5:16, Job 36:7, Ecc 5:8, Psa 71:19, Heb 7:26.

15252.text: M22 praise: Verses: Isa 52:13, Job 5:11, Deu 26:19.

15253.text: M41 being heard: Verses: Isa 58:4, Deu 28:1.

15254.text: M47 inner seat: Verses: Isa 57:15, 1Sa 16:7 (not the height of his stature; the Lord looks on the heart).

15257.text: Are any of the pride words indicative of God's characteristics? Yes: The gāʾôn family is used of God's majesty: "majesty", "triumphed gloriously", "robed in majesty" (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10); "Majesty" is used as a name for God (Heb 1:3; 8:1); The mocking words are used of God's derision: "He who sits in the heavens laughs" (Psa 2:4); "Toward the scorners he is scornful" (Pro 3:34); God is never the subject of a boast in these verses. He is its right object: "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (Jer 9:24).

15258.text: God's height is his own, shown in acts, and not overturned: "robed in majesty ... you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). "In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries" (Exo 15:7); Majesty goes with what only God does: abasing every proud one and saving by his own hand (Job 40:10–14); "God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7); Human pride, in the verses' own words, is a standing taken or assumed; "you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Gal 6:3); Mostly, pride holds as its own what was given; "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7); In story: Uzziah's strength, Hezekiah's healing, Nebuchadnezzar's God-given majesty, the cherub's beauty, the cedar's height (2Ch 26:15–16; 32:24–25; Dan 5:18–20; Eze 28:17; 31:9–10); This matches the researcher's "mostly assumed": the standing is real, but it is taken up as if it were not received.

15263.text: Given, then held as one's own: 1Co 4:7, and the kings' accounts. This bears on Ch 12 claim C-209, which now has much wider support: Pride against hearing: Jer 13:15–17; Pro 13:10; the scoffer who will not be rebuked (Pro 13:1; 15:12; 9:7–8). This bears on 10.2 Humility and hearing; Presumption: acting where not sent, speaking what was not commanded (Deu 1:43; 18:20). This bears on 10.7; Pride over others: the poor, the widow, the righteous; contempt; mocking the poor (Pro 17:5). This bears on 10.10 and OT-105; The boast moved to God, and boasting in weakness (Jer 9:23–24; 1Co 1:31; 2Co 12:9). This bears on Ch 12 claim C-182 and Ch 11 §4; Pride against love (1Co 8:1; 13:4), against rest (Hab 2:5 against Psa 131:2), and in place of mourning (1Co 5:2); The other face (2Ch 17:6; Psa 138:3; Psa 47:4; Isa 60:15) goes to Ch 11 §4, as a change of character.

15266.text: Turns toward help (Deu 33:26): Human pride: Turns away from God: "does not seek him" (Psa 10:4).

15267.text: Regards the lowly (Psa 138:6): Human pride: Stands over the poor and the widow (Psa 10:2; Pro 15:25).

15279.text: This is where the change-of-character reading (#1919) would start. No reading has been done: H1347 gāʾôn: human "pride" (25) versus God's "majesty" (9) versus "the thicket of the Jordan" (3); H1361 gābah: "proud" and "haughty" (Eze 28:2, 5; 2Ch 26:16; 32:25) versus "towered" and "higher" (physical) versus "exalted" of God (Isa 5:16) and of the servant (Isa 52:13); H1364 gābōah and H1363 gōbah: high walls and tall men versus "haughty eyes" and "a haughty spirit" (Pro 16:18); G2744 kauchaomai: "boast" versus "rejoice" (Rom 5:2–3, 11). Boasting in oneself versus "let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17); H1984H hālal: "boast" versus "glory" and "exult" (Jer 9:24, "let him who boasts boast in this"); G1702 empaizō: Jesus "mocked" in the passion accounts versus Herod "tricked" by the magi (Mat 2:16); H7292 rāhab: "insolent" (Isa 3:5) versus "plead urgently" (Pro 6:3) versus "overwhelm" (Song 6:5).

15281.text: What earlier strands already hold for M08: M09 (23 shared verses). These are the paired sayings, for example Jam 4:6, 1Pe 5:5, Pro 3:34, Pro 29:23, Pro 11:2, Psa 138:6, Job 22:29, Eze 21:26 and Dan 4:37. Most were read in the M09 humbling fan-out (#2148) and woven into 10.14 The proud brought low, the lowly raised; M47 (65 shared verses). Under the #1979 closure, each strand checks its M47 verses for dropped placements, by word and not by citation (OT-09); M72 (55 shared verses). Two group B verses are marked forward to M08: Eze 19:11 and Eze 29:15 (`m72-group-B-role-triage-v1-20261012.csv`). One group D verse names M08 among its forwards: Psa 36:11, "the foot of arrogance" (`m72-group-D-forward-v2-20261012.csv`); M18 (26 shared verses), OT-97 item 25 (`cluster:M08`). Two verses are marked forward to M08: 2Co 11:12 and 2Co 12:6, both Paul's boasting (`m18-group-C-role-triage-v2-20261012.csv`); M02 (20 shared verses), OT-103 item 22 (`cluster:M08`). These 20 verses fall across 16 anger faces. The list is the M08 rows of `wa-cluster-M02-mcode-face-combinations-v1-20261005.csv`; OT-05 item 16 (`cluster:M08`). Self-glory: "she glorified herself" (Rev 18:7) and "they glory in their shame" (Php 3:19). These are G1391 doxa verses (M22), held in `life-death-ot05-body-raised-groups-v1-20261014.csv`; Open threads matched (`Escalation.ps1 -Action Match -Cluster M08 -Strong <75>`): OT-05 (item 16), OT-97 (item 25) and OT-103 (item 22). No thread names an M08 Strong's or verse directly.

15284.text: Group A, the pride words (37 Strong's, 165 verses). These are closest to the inner act the definition names: the proud heart, haughty eyes, presumption, being puffed up: Group C, boasting (80 verses). Its main change of character is boasting in oneself versus boasting in the Lord (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10–12; Jer 9:24). 2Cor alone has 27 M08 verses; Group D, mocking and scoffing (76 verses). It covers the scoffer of Proverbs, the mocking of others (Elisha, the righteous), and the mocking of Jesus in the passion accounts. The scorn words are in M06; Group B, the height words (211 verses). Only 39 hits carry a pride-like surface; the rest are measures, places and God on high. This is like the M72 ruling (#1998): read by role, the height word is mostly a qualifier or a measure, with C (no bearing) for the measures. Those 39 hits are where B bears on M08; E (majesty) goes to God's character only (13.1). F is data; The words outside M08: self-exaltation in M22 and T3 (H7311A rûm, G5312 hypsoō), scorn in M06, taunting in M53, and "empty conceit" (Php 2:3) in T2. Under #1970 these are not re-tagged. Whether any of them is read with this strand is for you to say; What is already in the narrative: Ch 12 Pride and the lifted-up heart and spirit, 10.14 The proud brought low, the lowly raised, and claims C-207 to C-211. The M09 shared verses are largely read; What earlier strands hold:; 2 M18 forward marks (OT-97); the 20 M02 verses (OT-103); 3 M72 forward marks; OT-05 self-glory; the 65 M47 verses (#1979 check).

15285.text: 26 others: Gloss: | 45; Hits: | 1–4 hits each, among them H6277 "arrogant", H7292 rāhab "insolent", G5187 "puffed up", G5229 "becoming conceited", G0212/G0213 alazoneia/alazōn "arrogance", "boastful", G0829 "self-willed", G2755 "conceited", G4409 "preeminent" (Col 1:18, of Christ), G5367 "lovers of self" (2Ti 3:2), G5309 "haughty" (1Ti 6:17), G5252 "more highly" (Rom 12:3).

15288.text: H1363 gōbah: Gloss: height; Hits: 17; Verses: 16; Hits with a pride-like surface: 4 (Psa 10:4 and 2Ch 32:26 "pride"; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18).

15294.text: G1703 empaiktēs, G1701, G5512 chleuazō: Gloss: scoffer, jeering, to sneer; Tagged: T2 / T3; Verses: 1–2 each; Shared with M08: 0; Cited: 1; Surface that bears on M08: scoffers (2Pe 3:3; Jud 18), mocking.

15296.text: The height words are the same. gābah and rûm are God being high (Psa 138:6; Isa 57:15) and the heart lifted up (2Ch 26:16; Dan 5:20).

15298.text: No verse makes God the subject of a boast. He is the one boasted in (Jer 9:24).

15300.text: Height can be given: God gives majesty to a king: "the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar ... majesty" (Dan 5:18); He gives strength (2Ch 26:15), healing (2Ch 32:24), beauty (Eze 28:13–15; 31:9) and the power to get wealth (Deu 8:18); He gives his people a "pride": "He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob" (Psa 47:4); "I will make you majestic forever" (Isa 60:15).

15307.text: Pride is rarely alone in these verses. It stands over someone: the poor: "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor" (Psa 10:2); "Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker" (Pro 17:5); the widow: "tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries" (Pro 15:25); the needy left unaided: "pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy" (Eze 16:49); the righteous: "speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt" (Psa 31:18); the insolent who deride, smear and dig pits (Psa 119:51, 69, 85); with a closed heart: "They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly" (Psa 17:10); set against love, and among the things that divide: "'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up" (1Co 8:1); "love ... is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26); felt from below: "Our soul has had more than enough ... of the contempt of the proud" (Psa 123:4).

15310.text: The boast is moved, not removed: "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (Jer 9:24); "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31); The same word becomes joy in hope and in suffering (Rom 5:2–3, 11); Boasting in weakness: "so that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2Co 12:9); Boasting of others (2Co 7:4; 1Th 2:19); The boast within the measure God assigned (2Co 10:13), as thinking of oneself is within "the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3).

15332.text: It always faces someone: "before me" (1Ki 21:29); "before the Lord" (2Ki 22:19); "before the God of his fathers" (2Ch 33:12); "before your God" (Dan 10:12); Zedekiah's failure is put as "He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the Lord" (2Ch 36:12). Humbling before the prophet is humbling before the word he carries; Most verses in this group name before whom. Of the rest, 2Ch 12:6 and 2Ch 30:11 answer a word just brought, and Lev 26:41 goes with confession (26:40). Isa 58:3–5 is a fast addressed to God.

15333.text: It answers a word heard: Rehoboam and the princes humble themselves when Shemaiah brings "You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you". What they say is "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:5–6); Josiah humbles himself "when you heard how I spoke against this place" (2Ki 22:19; 2Ch 34:27); Ahab does so "when Ahab heard those words" (1Ki 21:27); Belshazzar is charged: "you … have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this" (Dan 5:22). He had the word, in his father's story, and did not bow to it.

15335.text: What it is set against: pride of heart (2Ch 32:25); "you have lifted up yourself against the Lord" (Dan 5:23), as his father's "heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly" (5:20); "He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning" (2Ch 36:13); "Do not now be stiff-necked … but yield yourselves" (2Ch 30:8), answered by mocking in some and humbling in others (30:10–11; carried); "How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me?" (Exo 10:3), said to Pharaoh, whose heart is hardened (10:1).

15336.text: What goes with it: saying "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); tearing clothes, sackcloth, fasting, going about "dejectedly" (1Ki 21:27); weeping (2Ki 22:19); entreating and praying (2Ch 33:12–13); fasting and seeking (Ezr 8:21); the condition "humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways" (2Ch 7:14); confession, and making amends for iniquity (Lev 26:40–41).

15344.text: A humbling God does not take knowledge of: Isa 58:3–5: The people ask: "Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"; The answer: "in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers", and "you fast only to quarrel and to fight"; The form is named and set aside: "Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him?"; The fast God chooses is turned to others: "to loose the bonds of wickedness … to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him" (58:6–7); Compare Ahab. His sackcloth and fasting were seen and answered (1Ki 21:27–29); I read: the outward acts are the same. What differs, by the two passages, is what goes with them. Ahab acts "when Ahab heard those words", against himself. In Isa 58 the fast is kept alongside self-pleasure and oppression. The humbling that is not taken knowledge of is one that leaves the seen poor unseen (58:7). This joins OT-105; 10.1, 10.7 and 13.1 already cite Isa 58:3, 5. The reading here is for the humbling side.

15347.text: The next chapter goes on: God subdues the nations (9:3), "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (9:4–6). This is why Deu 9:3, an H3665 "subdue" verse, is read here and not as war. The passage turns the subduing into a warning about what the heart will say of itself.

15352.text: What is brought low is named, and it is the bearing of a person, not only a rank: "The haughty looks of man … the lofty pride of men" (Isa 2:11, 17); "all that is proud and lofty … all that is lifted up" (Isa 2:12); "the eyes of the haughty" (Isa 5:15); "the pomp of the arrogant … the pompous pride of the ruthless" (Isa 13:11); Moab's "pompous pride together with the skill of his hands" (Isa 25:11); "your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2Sa 22:28); "the haughty eyes you bring down" (Psa 18:27).

15353.text: Its setting: Isa 2: a land "filled with silver and gold … filled with idols; they bow down to the work of their hands" (2:7–8); Isa 5: revellers who "do not regard the deeds of the Lord" (5:12).

15355.text: Who can do it: Job is told: "look on everyone who is proud and abase him … bring him low" (Job 40:11–12). He is told this as a challenge he cannot meet: "Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you" (40:14); "not from the east or from the west … comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:6–7); "he brings low and he exalts" (1Sa 2:7); "I bring low the high tree, and make high the low tree" (Eze 17:24); "Exalt that which is low, and bring low that which is exalted" (Eze 21:26), as the crown is taken from the profane prince; God "sets over it the lowliest of men" (Dan 4:17); "The Lord lifts up the humble; he casts the wicked to the ground" (Psa 147:6); "You save a humble people" (2Sa 22:28; Psa 18:27; "humble" is H6041).

15371.text: OT-103.44 (M02 × M09). 2Ch 12:7, 12:12 and 32:26 are read: humbling oneself turns God's wrath, in measure. Zep 2:3, Rom 13:5 and Job 40:11 are in this batch or later ones (Zep 2:3 is H6035, batch 2; Rom 13:5 is hypotassō, batch 5). The item stays narrowed until those are read.

15374.text: M47 (#1979 check, by word): the heart verses read here are 2Ch 32:25–26, 2Ki 22:19, 2Ch 34:27, Lev 26:41, Dan 5:20–22, Dan 10:12, Psa 107:12, Deu 8:2, 14, 17 and Deu 9:4–5. Their placements in Ch 4 The heart are checked at the cross-check.

15375.text: Already cited: 2Ch 12:7, 12:12, 32:26, 33:12 and 2Ki 22:19 (10.13, where humbling turns wrath); 2Ki 22:19, 2Ch 32:26 and Dan 5:19, 22 (Ch 4); Dan 4:17, 37 (13.1); Deu 8:3 (Ch 2); Pro 16:19 (Ch 12); 2Ch 7:14 (Ch 14); Isa 58:3, 5 (10.1, 10.7, 13.1). None is in a section about humbling, because there is none.

15384.text: The humble seek: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3). Those already called humble are told to seek humility. I read: in this verse humility is not a thing held once and for all. The humble keep seeking it, under the threat of the day of anger (2:2); "I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the Lord" (Zep 3:12). They are left after God removes "your proudly exultant ones" (3:11). They are described by what they do and do not do: "they shall do no injustice and speak no lies" (3:13); "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord" (Psa 22:26) and "you who seek God, let your hearts revive" (Psa 69:32). In both, the humble or afflicted stand beside "those who seek". (Psa 22:26 is the afflicted sense, group VI.).

15386.text: The meek, beside not fretting. "Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath! Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil. For the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land … But the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace" (Psa 37:8–11): The meek inherit what "those who wait for the Lord" inherit; Meekness stands where the psalm has just said "Refrain from anger … Fret not yourself" about the prospering wicked; Compare Num 12:3 (carried): Moses "very meek" where he is spoken against; I read: in both places meekness stands where another provokes, and the one who is meek leaves the answer to God.

15387.text: Psa 25:9 sits between "Remember not the sins of my youth" (25:7) and "pardon my guilt, for it is great" (25:11). The one who asks to be taught as one of the humble calls himself a sinner, and "he instructs sinners in the way" (25:8). I read: in this psalm the humble are the teachable, and the teachable are those who own their guilt.

15389.text: The noun ʿănāwāh (H6038, M05 by tag) is in four of the five verses: Pro 15:33, 18:12, 22:4 and Zep 2:3.

15393.text: Set against religious acts in three passages: the fast (Isa 58:3–7, batch 1); offerings (Mic 6:6–8); the house and the sacrifices (Isa 66:1–3, group III).

15398.text: A humble king. "Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey" (Zec 9:9): The next verse: "I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem … he shall speak peace to the nations" (9:10); The humble king comes without the chariot and war horse, and speaks peace. "Humble" is H6041.

15399.text: A king who rides out for meekness. "In your majesty ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness" (Psa 45:4). Meekness is a cause the king fights for, in majesty, with "arrows … sharp in the heart of the king's enemies" (45:5). I read: majesty and meekness are not set against each other here.

15408.text: OT-103.44 (M02 × M09): Zep 2:3 is read. Humility is sought "perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord". The item stays narrowed until Rom 13:5 (batch 5) is read.

15410.text: M08 Pride: Zep 3:11–12, Pro 11:2, Pro 18:12 and Psa 138:6 hold the pairing. It is checked against Ch 12 at the cross-check.

15411.text: M47 (#1979): Isa 57:15 (spirit, heart), Isa 66:2 (spirit), Psa 69:32 and Psa 22:26 (hearts), and Pro 18:12 (heart). Their Ch 4 and Ch 6 placements are checked at the cross-check.

15412.text: Already cited: Isa 57:15 in Ch 2, 4, 6 and 14; Isa 66:2 in Ch 6, 10.1, 10.9 and 10.12; Mic 6:8 in 10.8 and 10.13; Zep 2:3 and Psa 76:9 in 10.13 (Psa 76:9 also in 10.12); Psa 69:32 in Ch 2 and 4; Psa 37:11 in 10.1; Psa 22:26 in Ch 4 and 10.9; Psa 10:17 in 10.6; Job 24:4 in 10.11.

15420.text: Isa 11:4: God's act: "decide with equity for the meek of the earth"; Set against: the shoot of Jesse, who "shall not judge by what his eyes see" (11:3).

15425.text: afflicted: Verses: Psa 9:12; 10:12; 10:17; 22:26; Amo 2:7; Where the verse speaks of: their cry, their oppression, God not forgetting them.

15426.text: humble: Verses: Zep 2:3; Psa 25:9; 34:2; 69:32; 76:9; 147:6; 149:4; Pro 3:34; Where the verse speaks of: God's favor, teaching and saving, and their seeking and gladness.

15429.text: Psa 51:17: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.": What it is set against: "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering" (51:16); What comes before: "Deliver me from bloodguiltiness" (51:14). The spirit and heart are broken over the speaker's own sin; What it is called: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit". It takes the place of the offering; The next verses: "then will you delight in right sacrifices" (51:19). The offerings are not abolished. They follow the broken heart; This is a fourth passage where what God looks to is set against a religious act. The others are Isa 58:3–7, Mic 6:6–8 and Isa 66:1–3 (batches 1 and 2). In Psa 51 the contrast is the speaker's own, and the next verses take it back up; "Contrite" here is H1794 (M10). "Broken" is H7665 (M24/T3). No M09 word is in the verse.

15431.text: Psa 34:18: "The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.": Its setting: "When the righteous cry for help, the Lord hears" (34:17), and "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers him out of them all" (34:19); Here the broken heart is the righteous man's, under affliction, not over his sin; God is "near" to it. Compare Isa 57:15, "I dwell … with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (batch 2); "Crushed" here is the M09 word H1793A.

15450.text: H1793A dakkāʾ: Faces in batch 3: crushed in spirit, whom God saves (Psa 34:18) · contrite with the lowly, whom God revives (Isa 57:15); What differs: the only M09 word in the set. Both times it is God who meets it.

15454.text: What the parable shows: The exalting of self is measuring oneself against others before God, and listing one's acts; The humbling of self is owning oneself a sinner and asking for mercy, with the body following: standing far off, eyes down, beating the breast; I read: this is batch 1's "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6) and Lev 26's confession, made into a single prayer. Batch 1's fasting is also on the Pharisee's lips. Batch 1 found fasting can go with a humbling God does not take knowledge of (Isa 58). In Luk 18 it is again on the side that is not justified.

15459.text: Mat 21:5: "your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey". This is Zec 9:9 (batch 2) fulfilled in the entry to Jerusalem.

15461.text: What these verses say: Humility is directed: "toward one another". It is a way of counting others: "more significant than yourselves"; It goes in company: with gentleness, patience, bearing with, forgiving, sympathy and a tender heart, every time; It is named against: selfish ambition, conceit, haughtiness, being wise in one's own sight, and domineering; It is put on, or worn: "Put on" (Col 3:12) and "Clothe yourselves" (1Pe 5:5); It keeps unity: "harmony", "unity of the Spirit", "unity of mind"; It runs both ways in authority (1Pe 5): the younger are subject, and the elders do not domineer. Both are under one command to humility; Paul's own: in Act 20:19 humility is the manner of "serving the Lord", and it comes with tears and trials.

15462.text: In meeting someone who is wrong or opposed: "restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted" (Gal 6:1). The verse joins the gentle restoring to watching oneself. Two verses on: "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (6:3); "correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance" (2Ti 2:25). The correcting is gentle, and the outcome is left to God; "make a defense … yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1Pe 3:15); "Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?" (1Cor 4:21). Said to those who "are arrogant" (4:18); "to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people. For we ourselves were once foolish" (Tit 3:2–3). The ground of the gentleness is the memory of what "we ourselves" were.

15463.text: In receiving the word: "receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21), after "let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger" (1:19). This repeats what batch 2 found in Proverbs, where humility sits beside hearing and taking reproof (Pro 15:31–33; 18:12–13).

15465.text: Where it comes from, in three verbs: Given: "the fruit of the Spirit is … gentleness" (Gal 5:22–23). In the same passage: "Let us not become conceited" (5:26); Pursued: "Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness" (1Ti 6:11). It is pursued in flight from "the love of money" (6:10); Put on: Col 3:12 (group III).

15467.text: The blessing: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth" (Mat 5:5). This is Psa 37:11 (batch 2), between "poor in spirit" (5:3) and "those who mourn" (5:4).

15468.text: A reversal, and a boast turned around: "Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away" (Jam 1:9–10); "God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God … 'Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord'" (1Cor 1:28–31); I read: in both, the low is where God's choosing and lifting are seen. The boast is moved from what one has to what God does. The rich man's "humiliation" is something to boast in, because it tells him the truth: he passes like grass.

15470.text: Paul, brought low and lowering himself: "I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound … I have learned … to be content" (Phili 4:11–12). Being brought low is a circumstance here, met with contentment, "through him who strengthens me" (4:13); "did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God's gospel to you free of charge?" (2Cor 11:7). A lowering taken on for others' good. I read: this has the shape of Phili 2: lowered so that another is raised; "I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented" (2Cor 12:21). Here Paul is humbled by others' unrepented sin, and the humbling is joined to mourning over them. Compare Jer 23:9 (batch 3): the prophet's heart broken over what he sees; "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2Cor 7:6). G5011 here means downcast, after "fighting without and fear within" (7:5). God's comfort came through a person's arrival.

15471.text: Col 2:18, 23. G5012, the noun Phili 2:3, Eph 4:2, Col 3:12 and 1Pe 5:5 use for humility, is rendered "asceticism" here: "Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels … puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind" (2:18); "These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (2:23).

15473.text: I read: the humility-word here names a practice that inflates the one who practises it. It is the reverse of the humility Col 3:12 tells the same readers to put on, a chapter later. Compare batch 1's Isa 58: a fast called humbling oneself, which God did not take knowledge of. Change of character (#1919): one Greek noun names humility toward others and also a self-made severity that puffs up.

15479.text: M47 (#1979): Mat 11:29 (heart, souls), 1Pe 3:4 and 3:8 (heart), Jam 1:21 (souls), Jam 3:14 and 4:8 (hearts), Luk 1:51 (hearts). Checked at the cross-check.

15480.text: Already cited: Jam 1:21 in Ch 14; Phili 2:8 in Ch 2; 1Pe 3:15 in 10.12; Jam 4:6 in Ch 11 and 13.1; 2Cor 7:6 in 10.6; 1Pe 3:4 in Ch 1 and Ch 9; Col 3:12 in 10.7 and Ch 11; 1Cor 4:21 in 10.10 and 10.7; Phili 3:21 in Ch 2; 2Ti 2:25 in 13.3; 1Pe 5:5 and Tit 3:2 in 10.10; Mat 11:29 in Ch 11; Jam 3:13 in 10.6.

15488.text: Col 3:12–13: Humility named: "Put on … humility, meekness"; Beside it: compassionate hearts, kindness, patience, "bearing with one another … forgiving each other"; Against it: after "put … away: anger, wrath, malice" (3:8).

15496.text: The relationships named: the governing authorities (Rom 13:1, 5; Tit 3:1; 1Pe 2:13); masters (1Pe 2:18; Tit 2:9); husbands (Eph 5:22, 24; Col 3:18; 1Pe 3:1, 5; Tit 2:5); order in the assembly (1Cor 14:34; 1Ti 2:11); those devoted to the service of the saints (1Cor 16:16); leaders (Heb 13:17); "one another" (Eph 5:21).

15498.text: What it is joined to inwardly: "conscience" (Rom 13:5); "mindful of God" (1Pe 2:19); "reverence for Christ" (Eph 5:21); "hoped in God", and "do not fear anything that is frightening" (1Pe 3:5–6); in 1Pe 3:1–4 the submission of a wife is set beside "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (batch 4).

15503.text: Data: Tit 1:6 (an overseer's children "not open to the charge of … insubordination") and 1Ti 1:9 ("the lawless and disobedient", in the list the law is for). The word is listed in both verses, not shown at work.

15510.text: From this batch: Christ under whom all things are put (1Cor 15:27; Eph 1:22; 1Pe 3:22; Heb 2:5, 8) and the Son himself subject (1Cor 15:28; Luk 2:51); Jesus "made lower" and crowned because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:7, 9). The word G1642 elattoō (T3) is outside the pull. It also stands in "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Joh 3:30). Both are to be checked in the analysis; Christ as the example of submission under wrong (1Pe 2:21); The ground given for submission is Christ ("reverence for Christ", "as to the Lord", "for the Lord's sake"); The OT words read in batches 1–3 carry no submission verb of this kind. The nearest are Gen 16:9 (Hagar told to submit), Psa 81:11 ("Israel would not submit to me") and 2Ch 30:8 ("yield yourselves to the Lord"). The OT side of the analysis is to be checked against those.

15511.text: OT-103.44 (M02 × M09): Rom 13:5 is now read. Subjection "to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience". All six verses of the item are decided: 2Ch 12:7, 12:12 and 32:26 (batch 1), Zep 2:3 (batch 2), Job 40:11 (batch 1), Rom 13:5 (here). Luk 14:21 and Psa 10:14 went to OT-105. The item can close.

15513.text: Already cited: Rom 13:1 and 13:5 in Ch 8, Ch 11 and 10.13; Eph 5:21 and 1Pe 2:18 in 10.12; Luk 10:17 and 10:20 in 10.1, Ch 11 and 13.3; Rom 10:3 in 10.6; Rom 8:7 in 10.7 and Ch 12; Tit 3:1 in 10.10 and 10.3; 1Ti 2:11 in 10.10; Luk 2:51 in Ch 4.

15519.text: Eph 5:21: Ground: "out of reverence for Christ".

15521.text: 1Pe 3:5: Ground: "the holy women who hoped in God".

15529.text: G5293 hypotassō: Faces in batch 5: submit yourselves to God · be subject to the Father of spirits · do not submit to God's righteousness · the flesh cannot submit · subject to authorities, masters, husbands, leaders, one another · the spirits of prophets subject to prophets · demons subject in his name · creation subjected not willingly · all things subjected to Christ · the Son subjected to the Father · the boy Jesus submissive; What differs: who is under whom, and whether willingly. Freely and for a ground (to God, for the Lord's sake). By refusal (Rom 10:3). By inability (Rom 8:7). By power (demons, all things). Against its will (creation). And the Son, of his own accord, to his parents and finally to the Father.

15534.text: Jam 4:10: "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.": This is the end of a run of commands that begins at 4:6, "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble". The commands are: "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil … Draw near to God … Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning" (4:7–9); In this passage, humbling oneself is not one act but the whole movement the verses list: submitting, resisting, drawing near, cleansing, purifying the heart, mourning. "Before the Lord" names who it faces; The passage opens with the quarrels that come from "your passions … at war within you" (4:1). Jam 4:1–8 are cited across 10.6, 10.7, 10.13, Ch 11, 12 and 13.1. 4:10 is not.
