15640.text: I read: the main lines run through both testaments without a break. The NT quotes the OT on three of them. It repeats the words of two more without a formula (Psa 37:11 / Mat 5:5; and Pro 25:7 / Luk 14:10 in substance).

15642.text: In the NT readings, three groups are about how one stands toward others: humility toward one another (batch 4 III, 7), gentleness in meeting others (batch 4 IV, 11), and submission among people (batch 5 II, 20). That is 38 of the 77 NT verses: "in humility count others more significant than yourselves" (Phili 2:3); "Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another" (1Pe 5:5); "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Eph 5:21).

15646.text: The OT verses read have nothing of that range. The nearest are Gen 16:9 ("submit to her"), Psa 81:11 ("Israel would not submit to me") and 2Ch 30:8 ("yield yourselves to the Lord").

15648.text: In the OT the ground for humbling is God himself and his word: "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); "when you heard" (2Ki 22:19); "trembles at my word" (Isa 66:2).

15649.text: In the NT a new ground is named: Christ, and Christ's own way: "Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus" (Phili 2:5); "Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example" (1Pe 2:21); "out of reverence for Christ" (Eph 5:21); "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" (2Cor 10:1); "learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29).

15650.text: The source named also changes. Gentleness is "the fruit of the Spirit" (Gal 5:22–23), and the mind of the flesh "does not submit … indeed, it cannot" (Rom 8:7). The OT verses read name God reviving the lowly (Isa 57:15) and the heart being humbled (Lev 26:41). They do not name an inner source given for it.

15653.text: He is the ground and the example for humility toward others. Phili 2:3–5 makes "in humility count others more significant" rest on "this mind … in Christ Jesus". Also 1Pe 2:21; Eph 5:21; 2Cor 10:1; Mat 11:29.

15657.text: OT: God "looks far down" and raises the poor (Psa 113:6–7); "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly" (Psa 138:6); he dwells with the contrite and lowly "to revive" (Isa 57:15); "your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36; Psa 18:35); "I have been broken over their whoring heart" (Eze 6:9).

15668.text: God humbles, for good: OT: "that he might humble you and test you, to do you good in the end" (Deu 8:16); NT: "he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness" (Heb 12:10); "be subject to the Father of spirits and live" (12:9).

15670.text: Humility beside hearing the word: OT: "he who listens to reproof gains intelligence … humility comes before honor" (Pro 15:32–33); "humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" (Isa 66:2); NT: "quick to hear, slow to speak … receive with meekness the implanted word" (Jam 1:19, 21).

15671.text: The humble king (the NT quotes the OT): OT: "your king is coming to you … humble and mounted on a donkey" (Zec 9:9); NT: "This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet" (Mat 21:4–5).

15672.text: God lowering himself: OT: "who looks far down on the heavens and the earth? He raises the poor" (Psa 113:6–7); "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly" (Psa 138:6); "I dwell … also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isa 57:15); "your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36); NT: "who, though he was in the form of God … emptied himself … humbled himself" (Phili 2:6–8); "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29).

15674.text: Mat 21:5 (Zec 9:9): What it says of him: "your king is coming to you, humble".

15683.text: H8074G (shamem, be desolate) carries an apocalyptic register not found elsewhere in the M10 corpus: Daniel's repeated formula of the abomination that makes desolate (Dan 8:13, 9:27, 11:31, 12:11), tied to the desecration of the sanctuary and to an eschatological timeline (the 1,290 days of Dan 12:11). It is a different genre and referent, end-times sanctuary desecration, from the same root's ordinary prophetic use elsewhere, desolated cities and altars as historical judgment (Ezekiel, Isaiah).

15686.text: G0266 (hamartia) carries the most theologically distinctive material in the exercise: Paul's treatment of sin in Romans 5 to 8 as a near-personified ruling power, not merely an act: sin reigned in death (5:21), sold under sin (7:14), sin that dwells within me (7:17, 20), the law of sin (7:23, 8:2), slaves of sin (6:6, 17, 20). No other M10 family treats its concept as an active agent exercising dominion; every other family's moral-failure words function as acts, states or burdens, never as a ruling force with its own will. A qualitative outlier worth flagging on its own, independent of the family's broader lexical pattern.

15699.text: Avel and avlah (H5766A/B): in Ezekiel's repeated formula, when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice he shall die (Ezek 3:20, 18:24, 18:26, 33:13, 33:18). Injustice is a moral reversal from a prior righteous state, relapse and not a starting condition, unlike guilt's recognition-model or cruelty's other-attribution, which describe a condition someone simply has or falls into.

15700.text: God's own repeated self-description as one who does no injustice (Zeph 3:5, Deut 32:4, Ps 92:15) is the fixed standard the reversal of the righteous person (Ezekiel's formula) is measured against.

15702.text: H7806 (shazar, 19 verses, the family's single largest strong) is glossed to twist, but every one of its 19 citations is literal tabernacle-construction material, fine twined linen repeated almost verbatim through Exodus 26 to 39 (curtains, the ephod, the breastpiece, the veil). It is technical textile vocabulary, not moral language at all; with the chul codes it accounts for 28 of the family's about 98 verses, a gloss-text-grouping failure of the same kind as family R and G0073.

15703.text: H5753A/B (avah) makes the metaphor's two halves visible in one root split into two codes: the physical sense (bent, bowed down in pain and anguish, Isa 21:3, Ps 38:6) and the moral sense (the confession formula we have sinned and acted perversely, 1 Kgs 8:47, 2 Chr 6:37, Dan 9:5) are literally the same Hebrew word, split only for cataloguing.

15704.text: The justice and judiciary sub-theme recurs strongly: H5557 (salaph) and H5791 (avat) are both explicitly about bribery and perverting legal judgment (a bribe subverts the cause of the righteous, Exod 23:8, Deut 16:19; does God pervert justice, Job 8:3, 34:12), and H6127 and H6140 apply the same crooked language to justice itself (justice goes forth perverted, Hab 1:4; make crooked all that is straight, Mic 3:9). This is the third family, after D and G, to converge independently on judicial and legal-fairness vocabulary: corruption of justice specifically, not wrongdoing in general.

15707.text: The same crushing verb is used destructively of enemies and redemptively of the self, with no lexical marker distinguishing the two. H1792 and H1794 (dakha, dakhah, to crush) are applied, in the same handful of verses, destructively, of enemies and oppressors crushed in judgment (you crushed Rahab like a carcass, Ps 89:10; crush the oppressor, Ps 72:4; the wicked who crush your people, Ps 94:5), and redemptively, of the self, as the state God desires and does not despise (a broken and contrite heart, Ps 51:17; him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, Isa 57:15), where crushed names the humbled disposition that draws God near. The Niphal and Pual senses of H1792 include both to be crushed and to be contrite in one entry; only the referent, an enemy or one's own heart, tells which reading applies.

15708.text: H2555 (chamas, violence, 43 verses) is the family's real anchor, structural and social and not incidental: it defines violence as a filled-world condition rather than isolated acts. The paradigm case is the pre-Flood indictment, the earth was filled with violence (Gen 6:11, 6:13); the recurring pattern afterward is social and structural: false witness (Ps 27:12, Exod 23:1), dishonest commerce and oppression of the poor (Ps 12:5, Amos 3:10), and a garment of violence worn by the wicked as a visible attribute (Ps 73:6, Ezek 7:23).

15709.text: Isaiah 53:9, he had done no violence, uses this same word (chamas) as the Servant's negative self-defence, converging with Isaiah 53:10's crushing verb (dakha, the same family) in the same Song.

15710.text: This is the fifth family in the exercise to converge independently on Isaiah 53 (after guilt, transgression, iniquity and the bearing verb nasa): the convergence is now a five-family pattern (D, F, G and the guilt subgroup's H0817 and H5375J), so this Servant passage functions as a hub text across the M10 cluster's vocabulary, worth flagging as a standalone pattern and a cross-family note rather than being rediscovered in each family's synthesis.

15714.text: G3900 (paraptōma, trespass) is defined more by its remedy than by the act: it is Paul's central Adam and Christ contrast term (Rom 5:15-20) and is otherwise almost entirely a forgiveness-context word: forgive their trespasses (Matt 6:14-15, Eph 1:7, Col 2:13), not counting their trespasses against them (2 Cor 5:19).

15717.text: H6588 runs the same three-register split found in family J (unfaithfulness): its meaning block distinguishes transgression against individuals, nation against nation, and against God, the same structure as H4603 and H4604's against man and against God split. Amos's formula for three transgressions and for four (Amos 1:3 to 2:6) applies pesha at the nation-against-nation register, functioning as an indictment formula against foreign powers, not individual ethics.

15724.text: H7379 (riv) is a distinct, formal legal and covenant-lawsuit term, not domestic quarrelling: case at law, dispute in court, and repeatedly God's own formal indictment against Israel or the nations (Mic 6:2, the LORD has an indictment against his people; Jer 25:31; Isa 41:21). This is forensic vocabulary, structurally closer to family D (crime and injustice) than to the Proverbs strife nouns it was grouped with.

15725.text: This family is relational and covenantal, not individual-moral: its dominant shape is betrayal of a bond, and the same vocabulary serves, without distinction, a betrayed human relationship and a betrayed covenant with God. H0898 (bagad, 28 verses) runs both registers in the same small set of texts: even your brothers have dealt treacherously with you (Jer 12:6, a family betrayal) sits alongside the treacherous sister Judah set against faithless Israel (Jer 3:8, 3:11, the marriage-infidelity figure for covenant breach).

15726.text: Proverbs uses H0898 structurally, as a fixed class opposed to the upright, destroyed by their own conduct (Prov 11:3, 11:6, 13:15).

15729.text: G0646, G0763 and G0764 (Greek) shift register slightly: less about a specific broken bond, more a general orientation of impiety opposed to godliness as a category (Rom 1:18 pairs ungodliness with unrighteousness; Titus 2:12 opposes it to living self-controlled, upright and godly).

15739.text: H8442 (Isa 32:6) folds error into a cluster with folly, iniquity and ungodliness: deliberate, not accidental.

15745.text: Cruelty is defined by the absence of mercy, stated explicitly, not implied. Three of H0394's six verses use the near-identical formula cruel and have no mercy (Jer 6:23, 50:42) or merciless (Jer 30:14); Prov 12:10 makes the same point as a paradox, the mercy of the wicked is cruel, that is, even their gentlest disposition still qualifies as cruelty. Cruelty here is not a separate vice alongside mercilessness; the texts treat the two as the same fact stated twice.

15747.text: Dominating H6184's 15 verses, cruelty is the property of oppressors and adversaries named from the position of the sufferer asking to be delivered from them: redeem me from the hand of the ruthless (Job 6:23); a band of ruthless men seeks my life (Ps 86:14); redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless (Jer 15:21).

15756.text: Ezekiel 18:19-20 sits directly against the transfer reading in the other direction: it explicitly denies that a son bears (nasa) his father's iniquity. The same verb is used to assert strict non-transferability of personal guilt in one direction, while other texts in the same set use it for sacrificial transferability in the other; the input data does not resolve this tension and simply contains both uses side by side.

15779.text: asebeō (G0764) at 2 Pet 2:6: Sodom and Gomorrah made an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly, the paradigm-case citation for this whole family's condemnation vocabulary.

15780.text: asebeō's second occurrence is the verb form referenced in the Jude 15 cognate pile-up: deeds that they have committed, the act named by the verb, framed by the surrounding noun occurrences of the same root.

15784.text: asebeia (G0763) as a noun in ordinary case variation across most occurrences: Rom 1:18's opening indictment (ungodliness and unrighteousness), the pastoral-epistle warnings (2 Tim 2:16's more and more ungodliness, Titus 2:12's renunciation), and Rom 11:26's eschatological promise (banish ungodliness from Jacob).

15785.text: bagad as a finite verb form, narrating a specific act of treachery rather than labelling a class: individuals dealing treacherously with a specific party (Jer 12:6's brothers, 1 Sam 14:33's people, Judg 9:23's Shechem against Abimelech, Ps 78:57's fathers) and Israel and Judah dealing treacherously with God directly (Hos 6:7, Jer 3:20 twice, Jer 5:11 twice, Isa 48:8 twice, Jer 12:1).

15787.text: ma'al (H4603, verb) explicitly against God and the sacred, its own meaning block's against God and against devoted thing sub-senses: Achan's sacrilege against devoted objects (Josh 7:1, the strong's own paradigm case), national apostasy and idolatry (2 Chr 26:16, 2 Chr 12:2, Dan 9:7), and a wife's suspected infidelity handled through a legal-ordeal ritual (Num 5:27).

15788.text: ma'al (H4603) in the breach-of-faith formula tied directly to the sacrificial guilt-offering system: Ezra's post-exilic confession of mixed marriages (Ezra 10:2), Deuteronomy's covenant-renewal warning (Deut 32:51), corporate national unfaithfulness explained as the cause of judgment (Ezek 15:8, Neh 1:8), and the priestly-law breach-of-faith offense against a neighbor (Lev 6:2).

15792.text: Jude 15 stacks three cognate forms of this root in one verse: asebeia (G0763) appears twice (genitive, deeds of ungodliness and in such an ungodly way) and asebeō (G0764, the verb) once (deeds that they have committed), plus Jude 18's separate asebeia occurrence three verses later (their own ungodly passions). This is deliberate rhetorical intensification through repetition of one root across noun and verb forms within a single sentence, not incidental repetition: a cross-strong-within-family finding that only shows up when G0763 and G0764 are read together against the same verse.

15796.text: Ezek 18:24's H4603 occurrence renders guilty, not unfaithful or treacherous: H4603 is this family's own treachery-word, not the family H_guilt word (H0816 asham), yet the English surface here borrows guilt-vocabulary anyway. H4603's English surface across its 16 occurrences ranges across guilty, sin, broke or broken faith, unfaithful, treachery, faithlessly, acted and committed: eight distinct English renderings of one Hebrew verb, several of which belong lexically to other M10 families (guilt, sin).

15799.text: This family's marriage-infidelity-for-covenant-breach structure (H0898's treacherous sister Judah and faithless Israel, Jer 3:8 and 3:11) is the same figure driving family C_adultery's Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel 23 material: both families independently land on the identical metaphor from two lexical angles (treachery-vocabulary here, adultery-vocabulary there). Already noted in the #1680 pass; reconfirmed here with the added morph evidence that both roots show the same participle-identity and finite-act split.

15800.text: G0764 (stepGloss be ungodly, a verb per its own meaning block) has its 2 Pet 2:6 occurrence tagged with morph A-DPM, an adjective form, not a verb form, while its only other occurrence (Jude 1:15, V-AAI-3P) carries a verb morph as expected. The same strong is tagged as an adjective in one place and a verb in the other, for a strong whose catalogue definition is exclusively verbal: a data-tagging question, not resolved here: either the 2 Pet 2:6 span is mistagged, or this strong has an adjectival sub-use the meaning block does not document.

15803.text: H2342J and H2342K (both chul, split by sense) have real, coherent meaning covering dancing, whirling, waiting anxiously and writhing in childbirth. Their combined 10 occurrences are literal in every case: a whirling storm-tempest (Jer 23:19, 30:23), a spindle or dance reference in a curse formula (2 Sam 3:29), the voice of the Lord making a deer give birth (Ps 29:9), a sword raging against cities (Hos 11:6), and anxious waiting (Ps 37:7, Gen 8:10, Judg 3:25, Mic 1:12). None describes moral perversion.

15808.text: The body is named together with the spirit and soul as the whole person: your whole spirit and soul and body (1 Thess 5:23); holy in body and spirit (1 Cor 7:34); destroy both soul and body (Matt 10:28).

15810.text: The body is offered, and washed, with the heart: present your bodies as a living sacrifice, which is your spiritual worship (Rom 12:1); let us draw near with a true heart, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water (Heb 10:22).

15811.text: The body is a dwelling, and not one's own: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God; you are not your own, for you were bought with a price, so glorify God in your body (1 Cor 6:19-20).

15812.text: The body apart from the spirit: absent in body, present in spirit (1 Cor 5:3); the body apart from the spirit is dead (Jas 2:26); the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life (Rom 8:10).

15813.text: In Heb 10:22 (hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and bodies washed with pure water) and 1 Cor 6:19-20 (your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit; you are not your own; glorify God in your body), the verse joins the body to the inner act.

15823.text: In Isa 57:15 and 1 Sam 16:7, both marked by the M08 strand's group B scan, the height word is not pride: it supports M47 (heart, spirit). In Isa 57:15 the height word is God's own height, set beside where he also dwells; in 1 Sam 16:7 it is the outward thing Samuel looked at, the height of his stature.

15824.text: Isa 57:15 also supports M09 (the lowly and contrite): God dwells with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly and the heart of the contrite. The main operation is God's dwelling with, and reviving, a lowly spirit and a contrite heart.

15826.text: A heart that cannot be quiet: the wicked are like the tossing sea, for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt; there is no peace, says my God, for the wicked (Isa 57:20-21). This is the figure of an inner state: restless, unable to be still, throwing up what is in it. The book already has the arrogant man never at rest (Hab 2:5) and the quieted soul of Psalm 131, but not this picture.

15937.text: 9. Cross-cutting observations for Batch A [Claude reading]: Each component has its own feeling profile in the text, but they overlap: *Heart:* the widest range, including joy, fear, anger, grief, anxiety, despair.; *Soul:* strongly bitterness, longing, weariness, being troubled.; *Spirit (human):* troubled, broken or crushed, faint, provoked, rejoicing, and temper.; *Flesh:* trembles, faints, rejoices, and is afflicted by divine indignation.; The heart's state governs whether a feeling takes hold. A firm heart has no fear, a blameless heart no shame, a hardened heart no fear of God. A proud heart brings wrath; a humbled heart averts it.; Feelings pass between the inner seat and the body in both directions: glad heart → face; joyful heart → medicine; crushed spirit → dry bones; wine, bread, perfume, eyes' light → heart; meat craved → weeping; The divine Spirit is involved in feeling: it gives joy (1Th 1:6; Act 13:52) and grounds the absence of fear (Hag 2:5; Rom 8:15); it can be grieved (Eph 4:30), and it groans (Rom 8:26); twice, its coming is followed by human anger (1Sa 11:6; Judg 14:19); it is sent to heal the broken heart (Isa 61:1); Breath and wind tie feeling to the body and to God: the blast of God's anger from the "nose"; "fills me with bitterness" instead of breath; the breath that withers grass; despair's speech is "wind".; God is given the same feelings in heart and soul: his heart grieved (Gen 6:6), his joy with all heart and soul (Jer 32:41), anger executing the intents of his heart (Jer 23:20).

16039.text: 0. Data notes (short): No pre-filter applies. There is no M42, M61 or M72 in this batch.; Death — v3 note (replaces the v1 note). In v1 and v2 the death words were filed outside the M-codes ("die" in T3, "death" in T10), so §1–§13 read the life side only. After #1880 both also carry M25. The death side is read in §16, and the earlier sections carry Revisit (delta) notes where it bears on them.; Tags that would mislead in the delta: "the heart of the seas" (Eze 28:8) = midst; the "flesh" of an ox (Exo 21:28) and the "meat" pots (Exo 16:3).; Not misleading, but lexically marked (kept, read in §16): *nephesh* = dead body (Lev 21:11; Num 6:6; 19:11, 13, 18); *nephesh* = "willing" (Gen 23:8); the sea's "living things" (Rev 8:9; 16:3); "heart" as the ESV surface for *nephesh* (Pro 19:18; 1Sa 2:33).; Tags that would mislead a reading (noted, and not read as the cluster's sense): "alive / living" (M25); = "raw" flesh (Lev 13:10–24; 1Sa 2:15); = "fresh [living] water" (Lev 15:13); = "wild beasts" (Psa 79:2; Hos 13:8; Eze 39:17; Lev 5:2); Generic verbs in M23: "multiply" (H7235), "be able / can" (H3201); "meet / toward / against" (H7122) in M37: ordinary encounter, not foreknowledge; M71 surfaces used in other senses: "greatness" = arrogance of heart (Isa 9:9; 10:12); "descendants" (1Sa 2:33); "proceeds" (Act 5:3); "color" (Dan 7:28); "bring / lead" (G5342, M70): Mar 9:17, 20; Act 5:16; "heart" = "midst": "the heart of the seas" (Eze 27:27); "in the heart of the oak" (2Sa 18:14)

16042.text: Context Gen 6:5–13 → 8:20–21: [Claude reading] The diagnosis of the human heart is the same before and after the flood. 16085.text: What the sequences show [Claude reading]: The oath marks adherence at a cost.; Elisha's triple oath is the price of the double spirit.; The Shunammite uses Elisha's own oath against him. Her bitterness of soul becomes a hold on the prophet that he cannot refuse.; Uriah's oath by David's soul is kept against David's wish. The wine that should have lowered his guard fails (a failed threshold — Batch F §7). He dies for keeping it.; The oath by the soul can guard a life while refusing a life. Zedekiah swears secretly by "who made our souls" to spare Jeremiah's life. He then declines the life offered to him (38:17, 20), from fear (38:19). The oath and the refusal are in one conversation.; 1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1. A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.; The oath misused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).; Revisit (Batch H): God swears by his own soul: "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. They pledge their own *nephesh*.; An oath on a life, broken after a spirit comes (context 1Sa 19:4–12): Jonathan: "he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine … Why then will you sin against innocent blood?" (5); "Saul listened … Saul swore, 'As the Lord lives, he shall not be put to death'" (6); War again; David's victory (8); "a harmful spirit from the Lord came upon Saul" (9) [O]

For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die" (13); "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (14); [Claude reading] The others' weeping breaks Paul's heart but does not bend it. Readiness to die and a broken heart sit together. The ending echoes Gethsemane ("your will be done", Mat 26:42; §7.3). Here the friends say it, not the one facing death.

16176.text: Context Psa 116:1–9 — cry, self-address, deliverance: "The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me" (3); "Then I called on the name of the Lord: 'O Lord, I pray, deliver my soul!'" The soul is told to rest before the deliverance is stated. What follows is walking "in the land of the living". Compare "you have delivered my soul from death … that I may walk before God in the light of life" (Psa 56:13). In both psalms, deliverance from death is for walking before God.

16177.text: Context Job 33:18–30 — the soul near the pit, and the ransom: "his life loathes bread" (20); "his flesh is so wasted away" (21); "His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death" (22); "If there be for him an angel, a mediator … 'Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom; let his flesh become fresh with youth'" (23–25); "man prays to God, and he accepts him" (26); "He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit" (28); "to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life" (30); [Claude reading] One sequence moves through three components: soul toward death; the flesh restored; the soul brought back; The turning point is a ransom found by a mediator. This is where Job's book names the price that §5.4 found refused elsewhere.

16181.text: The watchman delivers his own soul (context Eze 3:17–21; 33:9): "if you warn the wicked, and he does not turn … he shall die for his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul" (3:19); If he gives no warning, "his blood I will require at your hand" (3:18, 20); [lexical; Claude reading] "Deliver one's soul" shifts here: from death to bloodguilt. The soul delivered is the speaker's, not the one who dies. It is saved by speaking the warning, whatever the hearer does.

16183.text: 16.5 "The soul who sins shall die" — death as accountability: Batch D and E read Eze 18:4, 20, 27 and 31. The death-words show the whole chapter as one argument, ending with "turn, and live" (32).

16184.text: The heart's condition as the cause of death — wisdom and sayings: "fools die for lack of sense [*heart*]" (Pro 10:21); "Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who despises his ways will die" (Pro 19:16); "he who fails to find me injures himself [*his soul*]; all who hate me love death" (Pro 8:36; Batch F §3.1); "The godless in heart cherish anger … They die in youth" (Job 36:13–14); "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecc 9:3) → "a living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they will die" (9:4–5); "Discipline your son, for there is hope; do not set your heart on putting him to death" (Pro 19:18) [lexical: *nephesh*]; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity. They lie down alike in the dust" (Job 21:25–26). Here the soul's state at death makes no difference to the outcome. This is Job's counter to the wisdom sayings above.; "I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart" (Rev 2:23). The death is the evidence that the heart is searched.

The high priest's consecration forbids it (21:10–12).; "All the days that he separates himself to the Lord he shall not go near a dead body" (Num 6:6). This is the Nazirite.; "Whoever touches the dead body of any person shall be unclean seven days" (Num 19:11); "Whoever touches a dead person … and does not cleanse himself, defiles the tabernacle of the Lord, and that person [*nephesh*] shall be cut off" (Num 19:13). In one verse *nephesh* is both the corpse and the living person cut off.; Num 19:18 (the sprinkling); [Claude reading]

16209.text: The Spirit sets the term of Simeon's life (Luk 2:26). His release is peace (2:29). His next words move to Mary's soul pierced and "thoughts from many hearts" revealed (2:35). One scene holds Spirit, death, soul and heart.

16217.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: Life is held in the breath and the soul, and it is God's to give and gather.; "Living soul" is shared with the animals. God's breathing is what marks Gen 2:7.; One decision of God's heart could gather every breath back (Job 34:14–15).; In the flood narrative God's heart changes while man's heart does not (Gen 6:5–6 → 8:21).; *rûaḥ* moves across senses within a single passage, and the passage uses the movement: Eze 37: carrying Spirit → breath → winds → "my Spirit within you"; Judg 15: rushing Spirit → one's own spirit returning; Jon 4: an appointed wind that makes the soul wish to die; Strength and hardness are one word. *ḥāzaq* is courage, hardening and the nerve to kill, according to what the heart is set toward (§3.3). This mirrors the tender heart (Batch F §6): neither softness nor strength of heart has a fixed moral value.; Revisit (Batch H §7.4): more words of this kind — *nāṣar* (keep the heart / the "guarded" wily heart), *šāmar*, vengeance, fatness of soul and of heart, *šāgâ*, kinship-flesh.; The inner components give way in order. Samson (Judg 16): the soul vexed; the heart told; the strength gone; the Lord gone; The strength returns only when asked for, and joined to the soul's consent to die.; Jacob (Gen 45): heart numb → spirit revived by words and sight.; The soul is what one swears by and what one bargains for.; Oaths "as your soul lives" mark adherence at a cost (Elisha, the Shunammite, Uriah) or protection with fear (Zedekiah).; Souls are hunted for bread (Eze 13) and "captured" by the wise (Pro 11:30).; Nothing can be given in return for a soul (Mic 6:7–8; Mat 16:26).; Eating and drinking recur at inner thresholds, now in three registers: the merry heart (Batch F §7); the heart sustained by bread before it is made merry (Judg 19:5, 8); the soul that blesses after a meal and wine (Gen 27:25); Also: the sad heart at a feast that turns to prayer (Hannah, Nehemiah), and the wine-threshold refused (Uriah).; Enticement and stirring show how other agents reach the inner seat: God stirs human spirits (Cyrus, Pul, the remnant).; God sends an other-spirit to entice through prophets' mouths (1Ki 22).; God allures and speaks to the heart (Hos 2:14).; Desire, gods and false teachers entice hearts and souls.

16218.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: The flesh is valued by circumstance: all living beings; mortal life lived by faith; Christ's own flesh; weakness; an orientation opposed to the Spirit. Joh 6 shifts its value within one discourse.; Life-hatred has two faces. The despairing soul of Job, Qohelet and Jonah hates life from exhaustion. The disciple hates it for another's sake (Batch F §3.2). The words overlap; the purpose differs.; Fringe worth keeping: the dead-but-assembled body without breath (Eze 37:8); Jacob's spirit reviving at the sight of wagons (Gen 45:27); Samson's two prayers (Judg 15:18; 16:28); Uriah's oath by the king's soul, kept against the king; the Shunammite turning Elisha's oath on him; Eli reading heart-prayer as drunkenness; "stumbling of heart" averted by Abigail; the lying spirit volunteering in the council; the idol told "Awake" with the verb that stirs Cyrus's spirit; Nebuchadnezzar's heart replaced by a beast's; Elisha's heart going out to meet Naaman's chariot; Isaac's soul blessing after wine; Revisit (delta) — the death side confirms and extends the life side: The inner seat can die before the body. Nabal's heart dies ten days before the Lord strikes him (§16.1).; At death the texts give each component its own verb. The soul "departs" (Rachel). The heart "does not attend" (Phinehas's wife). The spirit is "not retained" (Ecc 8:8) and is "gathered back" (Job 34:14).; *nephesh* names the corpse as well as the living creature (§16.7). What it names is the individual.; The death-wish belongs to the soul, and is seldom answered with death (§16.2, §6).; Food answers Elijah and the people. A question answers Jonah. Something to look at answers the people in Num 21.; It is granted to Samson in one last act. To Saul it is granted by a hand that is condemned for it.; Eating stands at the threshold between wanting to die and going on. This is the life-giving face of the eating threshold in Batch F §7.; The heart decides which death is just (§16.6, §5.4).; The law of refuge tests the killer's past hatred in the heart, and shields him from the avenger's hot heart.; Ransom is refused only for the life that took a life in hatred.; Where the law refuses a price, a mediator "finds a ransom" (Job 33:24). Love cannot be bought at all (Song 8:7).; Deliverance from death is for something (§16.4).

16219.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: It is for walking before God "in the land of the living" (Psa 116:9; 56:13).; Its turning point is a cry, a self-address to the soul, or a ransom.; "Deliver one's soul" can mean escaping bloodguilt by speaking (the watchman, Eze 3:19). The soul delivered is the speaker's, not the one who dies.; Fringe from the delta: the same consolation spoken to two dying mothers; Saul's "life still lingers"; the Amalekite executed for fulfilling a death-wish; Qohelet leaving the spirit's destination open; the oath of 1Sa 19:6 broken three verses after a harmful spirit comes; a dead king buried for his grandfather's heart; "eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" set against a call to mourn

16491.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

16492.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Unclean spirits recognise the Son of God (Mar 3:11) and obey him (Mar 1:27).; Spirits either confess Jesus come in the flesh or are "the spirit of the antichrist" (1Jo 4:2–3).; They must be tested (1Jo 4:1), and the spirit of error stands against the Spirit of truth (1Jo 4:6).; The Lord can dispatch a lying spirit (1Ki 22:23). Ministering spirits serve (Heb 1:14).; Flesh in relating to God: "All flesh" is humanity as it comes to God: all flesh comes in prayer (Psa 65:2), sees salvation and glory (Luk 3:6; Isa 40:5), and blesses (Psa 145:21).; Covenant is cut in the flesh, and its inner counterpart is the circumcised heart (§7.2).; Flesh vs spirit as powers: Isa 31:3; Joh 6:63; 1Co 5:5; Jer 17:5.; The "life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11) is the ground of atonement.; God is shown with his own heart and soul in these relations: his soul avenges (Jer 5:9) and he swears by it (Amo 6:8); he acts with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41); he wishes for a heart in his people (Deu 5:29); his heart recoils in compassion (Hos 11:8); his soul delights in the servant (Isa 42:1); he gives up the beloved of his soul (Jer 12:7); the priest acts according to his heart and soul (1Sa 2:35); Speech and the heart. The heart speaks inwardly ("in the heart", §1.3), is spoken to ("to the heart" = comfort, §1.4), and its speech either matches the mouth or is betrayed by it. Hebrew prayer is an act of the heart that may or may not reach the lips.; Fringe worth keeping: *kāvôd* as the inner self (§3.2) — a possible inner-being term outside M47; the soul asked to die (§2); the double portion of another's spirit (2Ki 2:9); the dying soul naming a child and the returning spirit naming a spring (§1.8); Isaac's soul giving the blessing (§12); Qoheleth testing his own heart (Ecc 2:1); the Gentile's heart-and-conscience law-court (Rom 2:15); the flesh-then-breath sequence of the dry bones (Eze 37:6–8); "gain the whole world and forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26); "transgression speaks [as an oracle] deep in his heart" (Psa 36:1); the heart with "highways to Zion" (Psa 84:5); "absent in body … present in spirit" (Col 2:5)

They are noted and not used in §4. → Ruling R2.; Sin-root verbs used for purification [lexical]. Phili 1:7 "confirmation of the gospel" (G0951) likewise.; Eze 42:20 "on the four sides" (H7307I *rûaḥ* = side / quarter) + "holy" (M61).; Job 26:13 "By his wind the heavens were made fair" (H8235, M61).; Pro 19:15 "idle person" (H7423B, M14); Isa 3:20 "perfume boxes … amulets" (*nephesh* "perfume box" + H3908, M14).; Psa 109:24 "my body has become gaunt" (H3584, M14).; Judg 19:5, 8, 9; 2Sa 19:7; Judg 19:3 "heart" beside "arise / delay" (M08, M09) — idioms: "strengthen your heart" = eat; "speak to the heart" = speak kindly.

The inner-speech content is kept as in §10.; Deu 22:26 "murdering" (*nephesh* in "strike him … a life") + "offense" (M56).; Lev 20:19 "relative" (*šĕʾēr* flesh) + "bear iniquity" (M56).; Nephesh = corpse [lexical]. *nephesh mēt* "soul of a dead one" = dead body. 16495.text: The Psalms formula "upright in heart": Psa 7:10; 11:2; 32:11; 36:10; 64:10; 94:15; 97:11; 125:4 ("upright in their hearts").; The upright in heart are the ones who are saved (Psa 7:10), shot at in the dark (Psa 11:2), told to rejoice (Psa 32:11; 64:10), given light and joy (Psa 97:11) and who follow justice (Psa 94:15).

16726.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Moral condition is predicated above all of the heart. The heart is: upright, whole, pure, clean or blameless (§1); evil, crooked, perverse, twisted, false or double (§2, §4, §5); proud / high or humbled / tender (§9, §10); It is also where sin is stored, engraved or hidden (§3.3). God tests and weighs it (Psa 7:9; Pro 21:2; Luk 16:15; Act 15:8). The heart is the organ that is morally evaluated.; The soul (*nephesh*) is the accountable person and the life at stake.; It sins, realises guilt, bears iniquity and is cut off (§3.1). It is the unfaithful party (§5).; It is the life that righteousness delivers (§1.7) and that sin injures (§3.2).; It is the innocent blood that is shed (§1.7). It is afflicted on holy days (§7.5).; At the limit it is the corpse that defiles (§8.2).; The soul is less often *evaluated* (righteous soul: 2Pe 2:8; puffed-up soul: Hab 2:4) than *answerable*.; The human spirit is evaluated chiefly on the pride–humility axis (§9.2, §10.2): haughty, proud, hardened, lowly, poor, contrite. Otherwise it is: without deceit (Psa 32:2); right / clean (Psa 51:10); faithful in marriage (Mal 2:15–16); trustworthy (Pro 11:13); holy or defiled with the body (1Co 7:34; 2Co 7:1); sanctified with soul and body (1Th 5:23); perfected in the righteous dead (Heb 12:23); weighed (Pro 16:2); broken by a perverse tongue (Pro 15:4); [observation, not a count]; Other spirits carry the negative moral adjectives. They are evil / harmful (§2.1, 15 verses), unclean (§8.1, 23 verses) and lying / deceitful (§4.1, 6 verses). They are the moral clusters' names turned into kinds of spirit.; In the OT some are sent by God (1Sa 16; Judg 9:23; 1Ki 22:22–23).; In the NT they indwell and are cast out.; The Holy Spirit is the positive counterpart, and the one against whom human sin is directed: blasphemed, lied to, grieved, resisted, outraged (§2.4, §4.2, §7.1).; Inner vs outer purity.; Ritual clean / unclean / holy vocabulary attaches to flesh, body and *nephesh*-as-person or corpse.; Moral purity attaches to heart, spirit, soul and conscience.; Several texts deliberately contrast the two: Psa 24:4; 2Ch 30:19; Mar 7:19–21; Heb 9:13–14; 10:22; Jam 4:8.

16727.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Conscience is the NT's named moral-awareness faculty. It can be clear, pure, good, evil, defiled, seared, weak or wounded. It testifies (2Co 1:12; Rom 9:1) and is purified by Christ's blood (Heb 9:14). It is frequently paired with the heart (1Ti 1:5; Heb 10:22).; The OT does this work with the heart: "David's heart struck him" (2Sa 24:10); "my heart does not reproach me" (Job 27:6).; The Levitical "realizes his guilt" (Lev 5) describes the same moment without naming an organ.; The heart deceives itself and is the source of evil.; It deceives its owner: Jer 17:9; Obd 3; Isa 44:20.; Evil comes from it: Gen 6:5; Mat 15:19; Luk 6:45.; Its evil hides behind speech: Psa 28:3; 41:6; Pro 26:23–25.; Pride deceives the heart that holds it (Obd 3), linking M08 and M14.; Flesh carries on from Batch C (§11.5).; OT: flesh is the ritual body and meat — clean or unclean, holy or tainted.; NT Pauline: flesh is the seat of sin (Rom 7–8; Gal 5:19) and the ground of false boasting (Phili 3:3).; Positive NT uses remain: "holy … in his body of flesh" (Col 1:22); "bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).; Wind and breath are the image of moral emptiness: iniquity takes us away like wind (Isa 64:6); the wicked are chaff (Psa 1:4); "wind and lies" (Mic 2:11); idols with no breath (Jer 10:14); the *hevel* + *rûaḥ* refrain (Ecc); Only the messianic "breath of his lips" (Isa 11:4) and the breath that conveys the Holy Spirit (Joh 20:22) are active and effective.; Fringe worth keeping: *nephesh* = corpse as the defiling body (§8.2); the "high heart" that is pride or courage depending on direction (2Ch 17:6 vs 2Ch 32:25); the heart that strikes or does not reproach — pre-conscience (§3.3, §9.5); sin against one's own soul (§3.2); the servant's soul as guilt offering (§3.6); lies that kill and keep alive souls (Eze 13:19); the spirit of jealousy that comes whether or not the defilement is real (Num 5:14); false humility of the flesh (Col 2:18, 23); the thorn in the flesh against conceit (2Co 12:7); Eliab misreading David's heart (1Sa 17:28); "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" (2Ki 10:15)

16728.text: 0. Data notes (short): Pre-filter — "Lord of hosts" (H6635B, M72): 28 pairs in 22 verses. This is a divine title, not dominion as a relation. The group is reported in §1.9, not dropped.; Misleading tags (noted, and not read as the cluster's sense): "choirmaster" (H5329 "to conduct", M76): 10 psalm superscriptions (Psa 9:1, 11:1, 14:1, 36:1, 42:1, 45:1, 53:1, 57:1, 62:1, 69:1). The M47 word belongs to the psalm body. The heading has no bearing on it.; "hand: power" (H3027H, M72): 49 verses. Mostly the idiom "into the hand of" (Jeremiah's "into the hand of those who seek their life"; Joshua's conquest lists). It is read as agency, and only where the hand acts on an inner component (§1.1, §1.4).; Quantity words in M46: "abundance / greatness / multitude" of iniquity or idols (Jer 13:22; Hos 9:7; Eze 14:4), "numerous" (Deu 10:22), "to no avail" (Dan 11:27), "good for nothing" (Jer 13:10), "retinue" (1Ki 10:2). None of these is about wealth.; Words in M76 and M26 used in other senses: "pity" (Psa 69:20) — *nûd*, a sympathetic shaking of the head; "intoxicated" (Pro 5:20) — *šāgâ*, see §4.2; "appointed" (Jon 4:8) and "count on" (2Co 10:2); "heart" = "midst": "the heart of the seas" (Eze 27:27).; "spokes" (Eze 10:12) is tagged hand.; The death words are outside the M-codes (see the handoff §3), as in Batch G.

16750.text: Esther — the soul reversed. Context read: Est 4:12–16; 5:6–14; 7:3–8.; Mordecai: "Do not think to yourself [*in your nephesh*] that in the king's palace you will escape" (4:13) → "if I perish, I perish" (4:16).; Then, at the wine: "let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request" (7:3).; The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking … Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther" (7:7).; [Claude reading] Within one banquet the *nephesh* asked for passes from Esther to Haman. Esther's inner reckoning ("do not think in your soul") is corrected first. Only then does she stake her life. See §7.6 for the wine-threshold.

16754.text: A reward for murder refused: the murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8) → David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The claim of vengeance on David's behalf is answered by an oath on David's own redeemed soul.

Context read: Act 8:13–24.; Simon "believed … was amazed" (13); "he offered them money, saying, 'Give me this power also'" (18–19) [D1]; "your heart is not right before God … pray … that … the intent of your heart may be forgiven" (21–22); "in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity" (23)

16761.text: 1.7 Kingdom — spirit, flesh, heart, soul (NT): "unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom" (Joh 3:5) [D3]; "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom" (Mat 5:3) [H1]; "if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (Mat 12:28); "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of … joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17) → §7.6; "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom" (1Co 15:50); "strengthening the souls of the disciples … through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom" (Act 14:22); "hears the word of the kingdom … the evil one snatches away what has been sown in his heart" (Mat 13:19)

16768.text: Testing heart and mind; vengeance: Jer 11:20; 20:12 → §6.1

16782.text: 2.2 The price of a life, again: "The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat" (Pro 13:8); "each shall give a ransom for his life … The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less … to make atonement for your lives" (Exo 30:12–16; context read) → Batch D; Batch E; "your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver" (1Ki 20:39) → §1.4; Satan: "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life" (Job 2:4) → "only spare [*guard*] his life" (2:6). Context read: Job 2:3–7.; "they have devoured human lives; they have taken treasure" (Eze 22:25); [Claude reading] Batch G §5.4 read Mic 6:7 and Mat 16:26 as a refusal to set any price on the soul. This batch shows the law and the narratives do set a price, and state it: a ransom in wealth (Pro 13:8); a half-shekel that is equal for every life (Exo 30:15); a talent of silver in a parable that turns into "life for life" (1Ki 20:39–42); Satan's axiom (Job 2:4) is that a man will give everything for his *nephesh*. The difference from G §5.4 is the direction of the transaction: a life can be ransomed within the covenant, but a soul cannot be bought back from God (Mat 16:26). See §R-V.

16792.text: Slavery transferred inward: "you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart" (Rom 6:17). Context 6:16–18: "you are slaves of the one whom you obey".; "present your members as slaves to righteousness" (Rom 6:19); "I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin" (Rom 7:25); "we serve in the new way of the Spirit" (Rom 7:6) [D3]; "you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but … the Spirit of adoption" (Rom 8:15) [X+D1]; "do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another" (Gal 5:13); "fervent in spirit, serve the Lord" (Rom 12:11) [H1]; "such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites [*belly*], and … deceive the hearts of the naive" (Rom 16:18)

16794.text: 3.2 The servant's inner sentence: "if that servant says to himself [*in his heart*], 'My master is delayed,' and begins to beat the … servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk" (Luk 12:45; Mat 24:48–49). Context read: Luk 12:42–46; Mat 24:49–51.; The faithful manager feeds the household "at the proper time" (Luk 12:42).; The unfaithful servant says in his heart that the master is delayed → beats → eats and drinks with drunkards → the master "will come on a day when he does not expect him" (46).; → Batch D §10 (inner speech). New here: the inner sentence is followed at once by eating and drinking, then the sudden arrival (§7.6).

16797.text: 3.3 Burden — who bears it: "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden" (Act 15:28) [D1]; "they cannot save the burden, but themselves [*their nephesh*] go into captivity" (Isa 46:2) — the idols, which have to be carried, and their carriers; "Take care for the sake of your lives, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath" (Jer 17:21) → §5.1

16808.text: 4.2 Going astray — five agents: The heart itself: "a people who go astray in their heart" (Psa 95:10); The spirit, with a way back: "those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding" (Isa 29:24) [H1]; A foreign spirit: "a spirit of whoredom has led them astray" (Hos 4:12) [X]; "The Lord has mingled within her a spirit of confusion … as a drunken man staggers" (Isa 19:14) [X]; God: "O Lord, why do you make us wander from your ways and harden our heart?" (Isa 63:17). Context 63:1–6, 15–17: this complaint follows the divine warrior's "day of vengeance was in my heart" (63:4) and a plea that "the stirring of your inner parts and your compassion are held back" (63:15). → §6.1; The loss of understanding: "He takes away understanding [*heart*] from the chiefs … and makes them wander in a trackless waste" (Job 12:24)

16813.text: 4.3 Guarding the way keeps the soul: "whoever guards his way preserves his life" (Pro 16:17); "Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who despises his ways will die" (Pro 19:16); "Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them" (Pro 22:5); The watchman: "if you warn the wicked to turn from his way … you will have delivered your soul" (Eze 3:19; 33:9) → §5.2

16815.text: 4.4 ◆ Fringe (M76): "Reproaches have broken my heart … I looked for pity [*someone to shake the head*], but there was none" (Psa 69:20); "you have disheartened the righteous falsely" (Eze 13:22) → G §5.3; "they have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isa 66:3); "Your ways and your deeds … it has reached your very heart" (Jer 4:18) — the consequence of the way arrives at the heart; "The dogs have a mighty appetite [*nephesh*] … they have all turned to their own way" (Isa 56:11); "Ephraim feeds on the wind" (Hos 12:1)

16816.text: 5.1 Guarding one's own inner seat: "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life" (Pro 4:23). Context 4:20–27 — the guarding moves outward: words kept "within your heart" (21) → "life … and healing to all their flesh" (22); keep the heart (23); → the mouth: "put away … crooked speech" (24); → the eyes: "look directly forward" (25); → the feet: "Ponder the path of your feet" (26–27); "take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget … lest they depart from your heart" (Deu 4:9) — guarding the soul means guarding memory; "guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth" (Mal 2:15–16) [U+H1; H1]; "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34) → §7.6; "restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself" (Gal 6:1) [X]; "Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart" (Deu 15:9); "Take care lest your heart be deceived" (Deu 11:16); "Be very careful, therefore [*guard well your souls*], to love the Lord" (Jos 23:11) — distance 0: the "careful" word *is* the nephesh phrase

16821.text: God | "guard my soul" (Psa 25:20); "Preserve my life" (Psa 86:2); "he will keep your life" (Psa 121:7); "your care has preserved my spirit" (Job 10:12) [H1]; "may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless" (1Th 5:23) [H1]

16824.text: The prophet-watchman | Context read: Eze 33:6–9. If he does not warn, "his blood I will require at the watchman's hand" (6, 8). If he warns, "you will have delivered your soul" (9). The watchman keeps his own soul by guarding others'.

16830.text: 5.5 ◆ Fringe (M74): "guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms [*bosom*]" (Mic 7:5) — the closest intimacy as the place for guarding; The Gerasene: "He was kept under guard and bound with chains … but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon" (Luk 8:29) [O] — human guarding fails against the spirit; the word of Jesus succeeds (8:29a); "who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places [*nāṣar*] … eat pig's flesh" (Isa 65:4); "they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh" (Gal 6:13); "guard the good deposit … by the Holy Spirit who dwells within us" (2Ti 1:14) [D1]; "maintain the unity of the Spirit" (Eph 4:3) [D2]; "I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes and be careful to obey" (Eze 36:27) [D1] — the carefulness is caused by the Spirit

16833.text: The persecuted prophet | "O Lord of hosts, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause" (Jer 20:12; 11:20)

16837.text: Jeremiah's sequence — context read, Jer 20:7–14: "you have deceived me" (7); "there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones … I cannot [hold it in]" (9); "my close friends, watching for my fall … 'take our revenge on him'" (10); → "let me see your vengeance … to you have I committed my cause" (12); → "Sing to the Lord; praise the Lord! For he has delivered the life of the needy" (13); → "Cursed be the day on which I was born!" (14); Jer 11:18–21 has the same prayer, and names "the men of Anathoth, who seek your life" (21).; [Claude reading]; Vengeance changes value with the heart that holds it. In the Philistines' soul it is malice. In God's heart it stands in one line with redemption (Isa 63:4). To the anxious heart it is rescue (Isa 35:4).; The prophet's heart does not take vengeance; it hands vengeance over. The friends want "our revenge" (20:10). Jeremiah asks to *see* God's (20:12). The handing over ("to you have I committed my cause") is what makes the praise of 20:13 possible. Two verses later the heart falls to cursing its birth (20:14). The inner seat swings from fire, to entrusting, to praise, to despair in five verses (cf. the despairing soul, Batch G §6).; What follows the divine heart's vengeance is complaint (Isa 63:15–17): the people ask where God's compassion has gone and why he makes them wander (§4.2).

16840.text: Context read: Job 32:1–3.; "he was righteous in his own eyes" (1); "Elihu … burned with anger at Job because he justified himself [*his nephesh*] rather than God" (2); "also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong" (3)

16841.text: 6.2 The heart as judge of the self: "Faithless Israel has shown herself [*her nephesh*] more righteous than treacherous Judah" (Jer 3:11) — comparative justification; "I do not say this to condemn you, for … you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together" (2Co 7:3); [Claude reading] The heart can condemn the self (1Jo 3:20) or justify it (Job 32:2; Luk 16:15). In both cases the text places a higher court above it: "God is greater than our heart"; "God knows your hearts". 1Jo 3 is the gentler reading: the self-condemning heart is reassured, not overruled harshly. In 2Co 7:3 condemnation is set aside because the other person is held in the heart.

16842.text: 6.3 Flesh and justification: "by works of the law no human being [*flesh*] will be justified" (Rom 3:20; Gal 2:16); "God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do … in the likeness of sinful flesh … he condemned sin in the flesh" (Rom 8:3); "manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit" (1Ti 3:16) [U]; "you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God" (1Co 6:11) [D1]; "unnatural desire [*other flesh*] … undergoing a punishment of eternal fire" (Jude 7); [Claude reading] Within this cluster *flesh* means three things: all humanity, which cannot be justified; the place where sin is condemned; and Christ's own flesh, which is vindicated by the Spirit. This extends Batch G §7 (flesh valued by circumstance).

16843.text: 6.4 Counting: "So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom" (Psa 90:12) → Batch B; "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isa 53:12); "Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied … make many to be accounted righteous" (53:11); "it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring" (Rom 9:8)

16844.text: Balaam: "Who can count the dust of Jacob …? Let me [*my nephesh*] die the death of the upright" (Num 23:10) — the hired curser's soul wishes for the end of those he was hired to curse

16848.text: 7. Cross-cutting observations for Batch H [Claude reading]: The warning: "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34).; The counter-statement: "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of … joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).; David's heart reads kings rightly. Both flights to Achish begin in the heart (1Sa 21:12; 27:1). The second follows immediately on Saul's oath and confession (26:21–25) (§1.8).; Voices addressed to the soul — beyond self-address (for synthesis item 1): Others speak to my soul: "Flee like a bird" (Psa 11:1); God swears by his own soul (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14); God's soul is burdened (Isa 1:14) and avenges itself (Jer 5:9); Fringe worth keeping: the king's heart read by Joab (2Sa 14:1); bitterness of soul as the recruiting ground of a king (1Sa 22:2); the queen of Sheba's mind filled and spirit emptied (1Ki 10:2, 5); Haman's riches "worth nothing" to a heart fixed on Mordecai (Est 5:13); the soul's "burden" as its desire (Eze 24:25); Moses' despair answered by distributing the Spirit (Num 11); the watchman who delivers his own soul (Eze 33:9); Eli killed by the word "ark" (1Sa 4:18); Mary keeping what she did not understand (Luk 2:50–51); the sons of Sceva mastered by the spirit (Act 19:16); Simon's money exposing his heart (Act 8:21); the good intention set aside overnight (2Sa 7:3–5); "he who seeks my life seeks your life" (1Sa 22:23); Balaam's soul wishing for the death of the upright (Num 23:10)

16850.text: Batch G v1 | §4 (oath by the soul) | Pointer: God swears by his own *nephesh* (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). Ish-bosheth's murderers answered with the oath "who has redeemed my life" (2Sa 4:8–12; H §1.4) | Batch G v2

16851.text: Batch F v2 | §7 (threshold) | Extended: Esther's banquets (Est 5:6–14; 7:7–8); Daniel's refusal of the king's food and wine (Dan 1:8, 15); the servant's inner sentence → eating and drinking (Luk 12:45); Luk 21:34; Rom 14:17 (H §7.6) | Batch F v3

16895.text: 4. Mutual abhorrence — God's soul and the people's soul (Lev 26): "his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence" (Psa 11:5)

16901.text: The Lord (filed under "it was the will of the Lord to crush him … when his soul makes an offering for guilt" (Isa 53:10)): "Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied" (53:11)

16903.text: Received by God (filed under "to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isa 57:15)): "I will not contend forever … for the spirit would grow faint before me" (57:16)

16906.text: Context Psa 51:10–17 — four spirits in eight verses: "renew a right spirit within me" (10) [H1]; "take not your Holy Spirit from me" (11) [D1]; "uphold me with a willing spirit" (12) [H1]; then teaching, singing and open lips (13–15); "you will not delight in sacrifice" (16); "a broken spirit" (17) [H1]; The psalm moves from a spirit to be renewed, through the divine Spirit not to be withdrawn and a willing spirit to be upheld, to a broken spirit that is itself the offering.

16909.text: When the Lord crushes the servant, the crushing is purposive and passes into offering and satisfaction (Isa 53:10–11).

16924.text: Judg 19:22–25 | They reach Gibeah | "As they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city … beating on the door" (19:22) | The concubine is abused all night (19:25)

16933.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: "let my soul die" (30); The merry-heart threshold is the penultimate step (G §3.6).; The counter-case: the sad heart at a feast.; Hannah "would not eat … why is your heart sad?" → prays "after they had eaten and drunk" → is taken for drunk → "troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul" → face no longer sad (1Sa 1:7–18).; Nehemiah: "when wine was before him … Why is your face sad? … sadness of the heart" → prayer → request granted (Neh 2:1–5).; The sad heart at the feast is also a threshold, but what enters is prayer, and the outcome is a gift (G §8.2).; Revisit (Batch H §7.6) — the threshold pattern extended again: Esther's wine-banquets (Est 5:6–14; 7:3–8): "as they were drinking wine after the feast" (5:6) → Haman goes out "joyful and glad of heart" (5:9) → sees Mordecai → wrath → "all this is worth nothing to me" (5:13) → the gallows (5:14).; At the second banquet Esther asks for her life (7:3). The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking" (7:7), and Haman begs for his life (7:7–8).; One banquet is the threshold for two outcomes: Esther's petition is granted; Haman falls.; The threshold refused at the heart: "Daniel resolved [*set on his heart*] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank" (Dan 1:8) → "fatter in flesh" than those who ate it (1:15). Compare Uriah (point 5).; The inner sentence comes first: "if that servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed,' and begins … to eat and drink and get drunk" → the master comes "on a day when he does not expect him" (Luk 12:45–46; Mat 24:48–51).; The warning: "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34).; The counter-statement: "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).; Revisit (Batch G v3 §16) — the threshold and death: Nabal's sequel: the heart dies in the morning (1Sa 25:37), and "about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (25:38). The dead heart comes before the dead man.

16973.text: False peace declared in the heart: "blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe [*have peace*], though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'" (Deu 29:19); "to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come'" (Jer 23:17); "saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life" (Jer 4:10); "who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts" (Psa 28:3)

16976.text: 10. Gentleness — the spirit as the manner of approach: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?" (1Co 4:21) [X]; "you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself" (Gal 6:1) [X]; "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4) [H1]; "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29); "receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21); "make a defense … with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience" (1Pe 3:15–16); [Claude reading] "Spirit" here names the manner in which one person comes to another (1Co 4:21; Gal 6:1) — the disposition [X] governing an encounter. Where gentleness is located in the heart (Mat 11:29), it is a settled character. Where it is "of spirit", it is the bearing brought to a specific meeting.

16982.text: 12.2 The heart devising and muttering violence — one verb, opposite content: *hāgâ* "mutter, meditate" [lexical]: "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things" (Pro 15:28); "for their hearts devise [*mutter*] violence, and their lips talk of trouble" (Pro 24:2); "conceiving and uttering from the heart lying words" (Isa 59:13); "Your heart will muse on the terror" (Isa 33:18); "those who seek my life … meditate treachery all day long" (Psa 38:12); [Claude reading] The heart's inner murmuring is the same act for the righteous and the violent. Its content (how to answer / violence / lies / terror) decides its moral character. The heart is an organ of rehearsal.; Also: "who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually" (Psa 140:2); "in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence" (Psa 58:2); "war was in his heart" (Psa 55:21).

16986.text: 13. Encouragement and building up (M52): "the church … walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied" (Act 9:31) [D1]; "waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him" (Luk 2:25) [D1]; "strive to excel in building up the church" (1Co 14:12); "building yourselves up … praying in the Holy Spirit" (Jude 20); "being built up as a spiritual house" (1Pe 2:5)

16988.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch F [Claude reading]: Relating to others is most often a matter of the soul.; Souls are knit (1Sa 18:1).; A soul loves, seeks and fails (Song 3; 5).; Malice lives in the soul (Eze 25:6, 15).; Souls abhor each other, even God's soul and the people's (Lev 26).; One loves another "as one's own soul".; The heart is where hatred starts and is spoken (Lev 19:17; Gen 27:41). It is also where the response to another's fall is judged (Pro 24:17).; The human spirit registers bonds and bearing.; It is unsettled by a friend's absence and refreshed by a friend's arrival (2Co 2:13; 7:13; 1Co 16:18).; It is the manner of approach — gentleness (1Co 4:21).; It is what the wise hold back and the fool vents (Pro 29:11).; Sequences matter more than single verses. Reading before and after changed the picture in six places: 1Sa 18 (Jonathan and Saul); Lev 26 (reciprocal abhorrence broken by God); Psa 143 and Psa 51 (the crushing chains); Judg 19 and the other merry-heart narratives (threshold states); 2Co 2 → 7 (the spirit's rest through persons); 2Ki 2 (spirit transfer confirmed by others); Meaning shifts with circumstance in consistent ways: *crush*: by whom, and turned to whom (§5); *tender heart*: to what it yields (§6); *good heart*: from God or from wine (§7); *love / hate one's soul*: well-being vs clinging (§3); *hāgâ*: what the heart rehearses (§12.2); *nûaḥ*: what rests in or on the person (§9.5); Inner states spread between people: the fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8); heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42); a lowly heart gives rest to other souls (Mat 11:29); a congregation refreshes Titus's spirit (2Co 7:13); the prophet's heart takes in the people's doom (Jer 4:18–19); Other spirits relate to people as occupants of a house (Mat 12:43–45) and as seizures between people (1Sa 18:10; Judg 9:23 in Batch D). The divine Spirit rests upon people and is recognised by others (Num 11; 2Ki 2).; Fringe worth keeping: the knit soul beside the seizing spirit in one chapter (1Sa 18); the heart awake while the body lags (Song 5); God refusing to complete reciprocal abhorrence (Lev 26:44); Jezebel curing a vexed spirit by a manufactured good heart (1Ki 21); the prophet's heart for Moab set against Ammon's malice of soul (Isa 15; Jer 48; Eze 25); past hatred as a legal criterion (Deu 19)

16995.text: 0. Data notes: Pre-filters from the handoff do not apply here. None of "Holy Spirit" (M61), "declares the Lord" (M42) or "Lord of hosts" (M72) falls in Batch C clusters. Nothing was removed.; "Seek my life" is one idiom, not inner seeking. About 40 of the 96 M83 verses are *biqqēš nephesh* — "seek (someone's) life" (1Sa 20:1; 23:15; 1Ki 19:10, 14; Jer 11:21; 19:7; 21:7; 22:25; 34:20–21; 44:30; 46:26; 49:37; Psa 35:4; 38:12; 40:14; 54:3; 63:9; 70:2; 86:14; Mat 2:20; Rom 11:3; etc.). Here *nephesh* is life as the object of hostile pursuit. It is reported in §7.5 and not mixed with the soul that seeks.; "Lacks sense" is "lacking heart" (H2638 + H3820A, d1): Pro 7:7; 9:4, 16; 10:13, 21; 11:12; 12:11; 15:21; 17:18; 24:30; 6:32; Ecc 10:3. H2638 "lacking" is filed under M18 Desire. It is a lack, not a desire. See §1.5. → Ruling R1.; "Pleasant" (H2896A *ṭôv*) is mostly generic "good / better". It accounts for 59 M18 pairs. The inner-being uses ("glad / merry / good of heart", "good to the soul", "better … in spirit") are kept in §1.6. Generic "better" is noted and not used (Num 11:18; Judg 9:2; Dan 1:15; 2Sa 18:3; Gen 1:21).; "Striving after wind" (H7469 *reʿût rûaḥ* "longing/pursuit" + rûaḥ *wind*, d1) is the Ecclesiastes refrain (Ecc 1:14; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6; 6:9). It is correctly a desire + wind pairing. See §1.9.; "Whole heart" is *lēv shālēm* (H8003 "complete", d1). It is filed under M34 Patience. In the verses it means an undivided, integral heart, not endurance. See §5.1. → Ruling R2.; "Contrite" (H1793A) is filed under M11 Turning. The verses are about a crushed spirit and heart (Psa 34:18; Isa 57:15), not about turning. They are kept in §8.4. → Ruling R3.; Misfiled tags, noted and not used: H6569 "refuse" = *dung*, read as "refuse" (M30): the flesh-skin-dung-burned sacrificial verses (Exo 29:14; Lev 4:11; 8:17; 16:27; Num 19:5); also Eze 32:5 "carcass" and Job 41:23 "folds of his flesh".; H0014 "be willing" filed under M30 because it appears as "would not" (1Ch 11:19; 2Sa 23:17 "he would not drink it"). It is kept only where it is the heart's or spirit's refusal (Exo 10:27; Deu 2:30; Eze 3:7).; "As you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2Ki 2:2, 4, 6; 4:30): an oath formula. H5800A "leave" → M30.; Gen 2:24 "leave … one flesh" → M30.

16996.text: 0. Data notes: Jer 4:19 "I writhe in pain" tagged H3176G "to wait" (M68). The Kethiv/Qere allows *yāḥal* "wait" or *ḥûl* "writhe" [lexical; verify]. ESV follows *ḥûl*.; 2Sa 18:14 "waste time … heart of Absalom" (literal heart; M68).; Psa 58:2 "deal out" and Psa 78:50 "made a path" tagged "to envy" (H6424 *pālas* "weigh / level") — M28.; Pro 9:4, 16 "turn in here" (M11); Luk 4:1, 14 "returned" (travel, M11).; "High places taken away" beside "heart wholly true" (1Ki 15:14; 2Ch 15:17; 20:33; 17:6; M11).; Jon 1:4 "the ship threatened [*thought*] to break up" (H2803 "devise", M64) — a lexical curiosity only.; Lev 7:18 "credited"; Exo 35:35; 36:8 "designer / skillfully" (M64). The last two tie back to "wise of heart" = skill (Batch B §2.1).; Col 2:1 "face" and Gal 1:16 "anyone" (G4561 "flesh" behind idioms).; Job 7:5 "my skin hardens" (literal body; M75).; Flesh = meat, appetite = nephesh in the Deuteronomy meat laws (Deu 12:15, 20–21; 14:26): "because you crave [*your nephesh desires*] meat" (d0/d1). This is the plainest place where *nephesh* is appetite. It is kept in §1.1.; Distance note. Positions are in original-language word order [verify]. d0 = one token carries both tags (e.g. Deu 12:20 "crave" = *nephesh* + desire; 2Pe 2:10 "lust" = flesh + desire).

17004.text: Soul yearns, spirit seeks: "My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you" (Isa 26:9) [H1]

17008.text: Heart-desire toward sin: "Do not desire her beauty in your heart" (Pro 6:25); "everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Mat 5:28); "God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts" (Rom 1:24); "flee youthful passions … call on the Lord from a pure heart" (2Ti 2:22)

17012.text: 1.4 The willing heart and the moved spirit — freewill: "From every man whose heart moves him" (Exo 25:2); "everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him" (Exo 35:21) [H1] — heart and spirit in parallel, the same verb (*nādav*); "All … whose heart moved them … as a freewill offering" (Exo 35:29); "with a whole heart they had offered freely" (1Ch 29:9); "In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered" (1Ch 29:17); "serve him with a whole heart and with a willing [delighting] soul [*nephesh*]" (1Ch 28:9); "My heart goes out to the commanders … who offered themselves willingly" (Judg 5:9)

17014.text: 1.5 "Lacking heart" — the heart as what is missing: "a young man lacking sense [*heart*]" (Pro 7:7); "him who lacks sense" (Pro 9:4, 16); "fools die for lack of sense" (Pro 10:21); "He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself [*his nephesh*]" (Pro 6:32) — lacking heart destroys the soul; "Folly is a joy to him who lacks sense" (Pro 15:21); "the vineyard of a man lacking sense" (Pro 24:30); [Claude reading] In Proverbs "sense" is literally "heart". A fool is not someone with a bad heart but someone without one: the heart is the capacity that is absent (cf. Batch B §2.2).

17038.text: 1.10 Evil desire of the soul: "the great man utters the evil desire of his soul" (Mic 7:3); "The soul of the wicked desires evil" (Pro 21:10); "the wicked boasts of the desires of his soul, and the one greedy for gain … renounces the Lord" (Psa 10:3); "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isa 66:3); "The Lord … thwarts the craving [*nephesh*] of the wicked" (Pro 10:3); "The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing" (Pro 13:4)

17051.text: Wind and Spirit that will: "The wind blows where it wishes … So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit" (Joh 3:8) [W+D3]; "prophecy was never produced by the will of man … carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2Pe 1:21) [D1].

17052.text: 1.13 Longing for the spiritual: "long for the pure spiritual milk" (1Pe 2:2); "earnestly desire the spiritual gifts" (1Co 14:1); "eager for manifestations of the Spirit" (1Co 14:12) [D2]; "I long to see you, that I may impart … some spiritual gift" (Rom 1:11); "The Spirit and the Bride say, 'Come.' … let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life" (Rev 22:17) [D2]; "things into which angels long to look" (1Pe 1:12) — beside "the Holy Spirit sent from heaven" [D1]

17057.text: 2.2 The intention of the heart: "every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Gen 6:5); "the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Gen 8:21) — said by the Lord "in his heart"; "keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you" (1Ch 29:18); "the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1Ch 28:9); "disclose the purposes of the heart" (1Co 4:5)

17061.text: God choosing with his soul and heart: "my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18); "I have chosen and consecrated this house … My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16); "God chose you … through sanctification by the Spirit" (2Th 2:13) [D2]

17063.text: 2.3 Choosing — soul and heart: "The heart of the wicked is of little worth" against "choice silver" (Pro 10:20).

17071.text: 3.2 Greed: "They have eyes full of adultery … They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed" (2Pe 2:14) — heart trained, souls unsteady; "their heart is set on their gain" (Eze 33:31); "the one greedy for gain … renounces the Lord" (Psa 10:3); "greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life [*nephesh*] of its possessors" (Pro 1:19) — greed kills its own soul; "destroying lives to get dishonest gain" (Eze 22:27)

17072.text: 3.3 ◆ Fleshly vs spiritual (*sarkikos / pneumatikos*): "I … could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh" (1Co 3:1); "the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin" (Rom 7:14); "If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material [*fleshly*] things?" (1Co 9:11); "spiritual blessings … material blessings" (Rom 15:27) — neutral; "not by earthly [*fleshly*] wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12) — with "the testimony of our conscience"

17086.text: Blameless soul-life: "I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life" (Job 9:21) — integrity with self-rejection; "Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright" (Pro 29:10).

17088.text: Patience given by the Spirit: "the fruit of the Spirit is … patience" (Gal 5:22) [D3]; "by … patience … the Holy Spirit" (2Co 6:6) [D1]; "praying at all times in the Spirit … with all perseverance" (Eph 6:18) [D3]

17092.text: 5.3 Forever — the inner seat and duration: "May your hearts live forever!" (Psa 22:26); "For I will not contend forever … for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isa 57:16) [H2] — God limits his contending for the sake of the human spirit; "who inhabits eternity … I dwell … also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isa 57:15) [H1]; "Do not deliver the soul of your dove to the wild beasts" (Psa 74:19)
